en: The first inquiry (*vimarśa*) of the *Vyaktiviveka* composed by Mahimabhaṭṭa, titled "The Refutation of the Definition of Dhvani," is intended to demonstrate that all *dhvani* is in fact included within inference (*anumāna*).
Having prostrated before the Supreme Speech, Mahima composes the *Vyaktiviveka*.
This effort of mine is directed toward those who are my equals; for there is nothing in this world that is truly captivating to everyone.
While the lamp of the world shines with its rising glory, some blaze forth, others blossom, and yet others close their eyes.

Whether our analysis of the words of the author of the Dhvanyāloka is based on correct understanding or otherwise, it will certainly lead to fame; for the mere praise of the great is itself a source of honor. (3)
My intellect, having never seen a mirror, is now suddenly prepared to pursue fame;
how indeed can it recognize its own blemishes when fashioning its various ornaments?

In the exceedingly dense path of poetic resonance (dhvani), it is easy for speech to stumble at every step when it proceeds with impetuosity without having first seen the illuminating moonlight [of the treatise]. (5)
But noble persons, disregarding that [fault], should always be attentive toward even a mere fragment of virtue;
or else, like winnowing fans, they are by their very nature untrained in grasping the chaff. (6)

In this regard, the definition of *dhvani* itself must first be stated: what is this thing called *dhvani*? And that has been stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* as follows: "That particular kind of poetry in which either the meaning or the word, having subordinated their own literal sense, manifest that [intended] meaning, is called *dhvani* by the wise. When this is analyzed, it is consistent only with inference (*anumāna*) and nothing else. For instance, the subordination of the meaning’s own nature is simply untenable.

For that [word] which is employed for the purpose of conveying another meaning does not deviate from it; indeed, when smoke and the like are employed for the sake of establishing fire and so forth, they do not transcend the status of being subordinate (*guṇatā*), because their definition consists solely in that [subordination]. As for the claim that this [suggested sense] is sometimes primary in instances such as *samāsokti* (synecdoche), that is only with respect to its being the contextual subject (*prākaraṇikatva*), and not with respect to its being the suggested sense (*pratīyamāna*). For example: "The face of night was grasped by the moon with passion aroused and with trembling pupils."

"Just as she did not notice the entire garment of darkness slipping away before her due to passion. Here, indeed, it is the expressed meaning itself, supported by the suggested meaning, that is perceived as predominant; for the sentence-meaning consists precisely of the night and the moon, upon which the behaviors of a heroine and a hero have been superimposed. And because the suggested element functions as a mark (liṅga) in relation to that [expressed meaning], its subordination is invariable.

Even if there were variability, this [suggested element] would be dispensable due to its lack of efficacy; furthermore, it will be stated that even in poetry where the suggested is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), a superior degree of beauty is observed.
It has been stated that the quality of having its own nature subordinated [to another] is a qualification of the object;
however, because it is invariably concomitant with the capacity to convey meaning, that [qualification] is not appropriate for it. (7)

This is the summary verse. Furthermore, the word itself is certainly not something to be adopted [as a primary object]. This is because it will be demonstrated that no other function for it is possible except for the denotation of its own meaning. Nor is it possible for it to have its meaning subordinated [to another] except in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), as in the following example: "Having approached the root of his ear under the guise of grey hair, Old Age said, 'O Kaikeyī, let sovereignty be placed upon Rāma,' suspecting her to be Kaikeyī herself. Thus [ends the discussion].

From what, then, does the comprehension of that meaning arise? We say it arises from the *anukārya* (the original object being imitated), because that [object] is twofold, distinguished by being either meaningful (*sārthaka*) or meaningless (*nirarthaka*). It does not arise from the *anukaraṇa* (the imitation itself), for that, being delimited by the particle *iti*, abides in its own form alone. As for any other [word], there is no deviation from its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), since it is employed for the sake of that [original object]. For it is not reasonable to say that whatever is employed for the sake of something else would itself make that very thing subordinate.

Just as a jar or the like is taken up for the purpose of obtaining water and so forth, yet the water itself is not [the primary object]; otherwise, the distinction between the primary and the secondary would be entirely without foundation. For this very reason, it is impossible that the jar and such alone should be substituted while the water and such are not; thus, "impossibility" (*asambhava*) is a defect of the definition (*lakṣaṇadoṣa*). Furthermore, the statement regarding the subordination of their own meanings even when deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and possibility (*sambhava*) are present is redundant, because it has already been stated that since those two are employed for the sake of manifesting another meaning, that [subordination] is understood through their very capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Nor can it be said that this has as its fruit merely the restatement of the essential nature [of the subject], because that would result in the fallacy of tautology. Thus, one should understand that the examples cited, such as "Three kinds of men gather the golden-flowered earth: the hero, the man of learning, and he who knows how to serve," are characterized by a probandum (sādhya) and a probans (sādhana) whose properties are not yet established.

Furthermore, just as the object denoted and its qualifiers are presented, so too must the expression (abhidhā) itself be presented. Otherwise, in cases where another ornament such as *dīpaka* is perceived through [the presence of] another ornament such as *upamā*, it would not be desired that these constitute *dhvani*, because they would be excluded by the definition [of *dhvani*]. Moreover, the nature of ornaments has been accepted as consisting of direct denotation (*abhidhātmatva*), since they take the form of specific varieties of figurative speech (*bhaṅgībhaṇiti*). This applies even when another ornament is being manifested.

If it is argued that this has been refuted by such statements as, "The primary intent does not belong to the expressed meaning; this is not considered the path of *dhvani*," we reply: that refutation is invalid because its reason—the criterion of being "not primarily intent on the expressed"—is unestablished. This is because [the verse] relies solely on the employment of stylistic devices (*bhaṅgībhaṇiti*) such as *dīpaka* and other ornaments, which are primarily intent on expressing the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*). Furthermore, since the suggested ornament and so forth possess a superior degree of beauty, and since the designation of *dhvani* is based precisely upon that [suggested beauty], how can the refutation stand?

Is its negation established [by inference]? Or rather, is its existence understood precisely because the cognition of the object would otherwise be impossible? Furthermore, since the words [denoting] the object and the word itself have the capacity to express their own meanings while subordinating those meanings, there is an understanding of that subordination. If it were the case that their subordination [to the cognition] occurs primarily through that [cognition], then the consequence would be that the employment of those two [the object and the word] would be useless.

In that case, it is the meaning alone that becomes subordinate, not the word; for the cognition of that [word] is established simply by the capacity of the denotation itself to indicate its own subordination, just as in the case of the denotation. Thus, the inclusion of the term "word" (*śabda*) in the definition-sentence is redundant. Otherwise, one would also have to include the term "denotation" (*abhidhāna*), as there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Furthermore, for this [word], whose capacity is exhausted merely by the denotation of its own primary meaning, no other operation is logically possible by which it might cause another object to be understood; nor could it, depending on that [other operation], become subordinate in its own meaning. For it is the object itself that possesses the capacity to bring about that [understanding]. Indeed, every verbal transaction must generally be accepted as being of the nature of inference, since it is essentially grounded in the relationship between the probandum and the probans.

This is because it serves as the basis for the engagement with or withdrawal from another, and because those two—consisting of conviction and lack of conviction—cannot be otherwise produced. For no discerning person becomes a possessor of conviction based on mere words without understanding the underlying reasoning. Indeed, speech is of two kinds, distinguished as *pada* (word) and *vākya* (sentence). Among these, the word (*pada*) is of many types, distinguished as noun (*nāman*), verb (*ākhyāta*), prefix (*upasarga*), particle (*nipāta*), and prepositional adverb (*karmapravacanīya*). Among these, nouns (*nāman*) are primarily concerned with substance (*sattva*).

These [words] also arise in many varieties, because there are many bases for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*). For example: "jar" and "cloth" are words for genus; "white" and "blue" are words for quality; "cook" and "reader" are words for action; and "staff-bearer" and "horned one" are words for substance. However, some maintain that action alone is the single basis for the application of all these nominal words, and thus they accept that all nouns are exclusively words for action.

For instance, words such as "jar" (ghaṭa), when applied to their own referents, are seen to rely—by way of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—exclusively upon the action of "jarring" (*ghaṭana*) as the ground for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*). They do not rely on the universal (*sāmānya*) of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). And let this action of jarring be either due to its connection with the universal of jar-ness or otherwise; this much does not undermine its status as the ground for application.

Moreover, even though the universal "pot-ness" exists, that which is itself not a pot, failing to attain the nature of a pot, cannot be the referent of the designation "pot. For if it were so, even a cloth would become the referent of the designation "pot," since there would be no distinction in its being a non-agent of the action of "pot-making. Indeed, an object that does not attain whiteness cannot be designated as "white," nor can one who is not cooking be called a "cook."

Therefore, it should be understood that the very definition of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*)—characterized by being the agent of the action of forming—is the cause for the application of the word "pot," and not merely "pot-ness" in abstraction. And that [action] itself is what is referred to here as "forming" (*ghaṭana*). [Objection: But surely, we also accept that for all words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), the cause for their application is simply the action of forming (*ghaṭanādi-kriyā*) derived from verbal roots like *ghaṭ* (meaning "to form") when followed by suffixes such as *aj* (e.g., in the sense of "it forms," *ghaṭate*). Thus, the presentation of this alternative view is redundant. [Reply: True, you do indeed accept this.

However, that [quality] is the etymological ground (*vyutpattinimitta*) of the word, not its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). For the etymological ground is one thing, and the ground for application is another. According to the view of some, the action of going and so forth is the etymological ground of words such as "cow" (*go*), while the universal "cowness" (*gotva*)—through its inherence in the same object—functions as the ground for application. It is for this reason that the word "cow" is established as applicable whether the cow is moving or not moving.

In the same way, it is established here as well that activity such as "shaping" (*ceṣṭā*) is the basis for the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-nimitta*) of words like "jar" (*ghaṭa*). Furthermore, in expressions such as "having ripened, it becomes a jar," it should be understood that the priority of the action of ripening (*vipākādi-kriyā*)—relative to that very [action of becoming]—is the domain of the suffix *-ktvā*. This is just as in expressions like "having placed [the pot] on the fire, he becomes a cook," where the priority of the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is relative to the cooking (*pāka*), and not relative to the action of becoming (*bhavana-kriyā*); for the latter is not necessarily employed [as a verbalized action], yet it is nevertheless understood because the existence (*sattā*) of things is never absent.

However, one should not think that [the action] is dependent on that [subsequent action] merely for that reason, because the latter is external and because it would result in a lack of logical connection with the meaning. Furthermore, the temporal priority denoted by the suffix *ktvā* generally refers to dependence upon the action actually expressed, not upon that which is merely implied; otherwise, one might say, "even after hearing, the deaf man [remains deaf]," or "even after seeing, the blind man [remains blind]," or "even after knowing, the dull-witted man [remains ignorant]. Only he who acts in consideration of place, time, and purpose is truly a wise man.

Such a series of logical applications would indeed be untenable, because hearing and the other [senses] would lack priority in time relative to that [cognition]. However, in this case, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, as the priority of hearing and the others is contingent solely upon actions such as deafness, which is characterized by a deficiency in the capacity for hearing and so forth. Furthermore, among those many [actions], the priority of each preceding action is contingent upon each succeeding action, as in the examples: "having bathed, having eaten, having drunk, he goes," and so on.

And here, although there are many actions consisting of the forms of ripening (*vipacana*), pot-making (*ghaṭana*), and becoming (*bhavana*), it is indeed possible for the ripening to have [the same agent] in relation to the pot-making, since there is no difference in the designation of the agent by the suffix in both cases. It is only because the agent has been reduced to the status of a limiting attribute (*upādhi*) by being expressed through a *kṛt* suffix that the delusion arises that they have different agents. For example: "Setting aside the cold season, what quality of ours is there like the warmth of the chest of this dispeller of cold?"

"Thus, with this thought, the beloveds embraced the lover who was bent down and submissive after he had been struck. In this verse, the action of "taking away" belongs to the agent, which is the heat of the breasts; for this very reason, some have explained that *apāsya* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that functions as a substitute for a gerund (*lyabantapratirūpaka*). Or, for example: "Having observed the son of Rādhā (Karṇa), whose fortitude was cast aside by his fury and who had propitiated Jamadagni’s son (Paraśurāma)—even Death himself might show partiality toward those who are unprepared for sudden fears."

In this [first example], the action of falling into the lap of Death—the agent of the act of looking—is presented through the device of the relationship between the object and the subject. Or, for example: "Even after seeing her, no other [woman] finds a place in my mind, which is full of longing. Here, the mind—which is the agent of the act of seeing—is presented as the non-substratum (anadhikaraṇa) of the act of finding a place performed by another agent; thus, the act of longing is presented as a qualifier of that [mind]. In some cases, this [qualifier] comes to possess a relationship with the agent.

An example of a cause based on delusion (*bhrama-hetu*) is as follows: "Having prostrated with my head, having been entreated, and having embraced you while trembling—remembering those secret amorous acts of yours, O Smara, I find no peace. Some, however, maintain that a cause may also consist in the non-mention of either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the action (*kriyā*). An example of the non-mention of the agent is as follows: "Indeed, everyone attains honor only after perceiving some merit; what merit, O Lord of the Kurus, can there be in the worship of Hari, who is devoid of all merit?"

For here, there is a single agent for both "observing" (*samavekṣā*) and "worshipping" (*pūjā*); since that [agent] is established by implication, it is not explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, although "worship" (*pūjā*) is mentioned, because it is expressed by a primary suffix (*kṛt*), its object becomes subordinate; thus, both of these are causes for confusion. As in the case of an action: "Without causing distress to others, without resorting to base servility, and without abandoning the path of the virtuous, whatever [one does], even if very little, is much. For here, the non-mention of the act of "gaining" (*lābha*), which is understood from the context and so forth, is the cause for the confusion that the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors have different agents.

Thus it has been said: "The suffix *ktvā*, whether expressed as denoting the agent through its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or having attained the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇatā*), serves to create the illusion of a difference in agents between two actions. When one relies on the actual temporal sequence of actions, what is the need for considering their primacy or subordination regarding the priority [expressed by] *ktvā*? Enough of this.
A pot is to be known as that which "pot-acts" (*ghaṭati*); that which does not act as a pot cannot attain the state of being a pot.
Otherwise, even a cloth would be a pot, since there would be no distinction from the state of non-potness. (8)
And "joining" (ghaṭana) is considered an activity consisting in the attainment of that [divine] nature;
and its root is the manifestation of the appearance of variegated objects by the Lord. ||9||
Whatever meaning may serve as the basis for the derivation of words, in their actual usage, there is only action, characterized by the attainment of existence. (10)
In that very [context], the *kvip* suffix and others are to be applied based solely on the agent;
however, they are not applied to the object of comparison in the sense of "behaving like," because those two meanings are already understood from the context. (11)
For just as from the statement "the donkey eats" this meaning is understood, yet by implication the meaning "the donkey attains the state of being a horse" is further conveyed. (12)
One who behaves like a horse is judged to be a donkey; for it is not right to apply that designation to one whose actions are not equal to those [of a horse]. (13)

And this activity within existence is possible even for an insentient thing like a jar, because it is established through its own manifoldness, just as the act of being a jar and so forth [is possible for a jar]. (14)
For this very reason, Pāṇini, whose name is primarily associated with "sattva" (being), declared that the meaning of a verbal root consists of a portion of the speech-path and so forth. 15.
And thus, in the expression "having ripened in this way, it becomes a jar," the suffix -ktvā indicates its anteriority [to the action of becoming].

This should be understood as being relative to the act of forming (ghaṭana), but not relative to the act of existing (bhavana), because there is no concomitance [of the former with the latter]. ||16||
And because it is external, as in the case of "this man is a cook having placed [the pot] on the fire.
For here, there is an understanding of the priority of time for the act of placing on the fire with respect to the act of cooking. ||17||
Therefore, whatever meaning is understood from names and words, it cannot be expressed by speech without having attained existence (sattā). ||18||
And thus, verbs such as *asti* (is) and *bhavati* (becomes) express general action; however, speakers do not necessarily employ them because of their internal nature. (19)
As for any other specific action, such as cooking and the like, which is subject to deviation, its employment must necessarily be admitted due to its being extrinsic (bahiraṅga). ||20||

These are the summary verses. A verb (ākhyāta) has action (bhāva) as its primary meaning. Prefixes (upasarga) and the like have meanings that are not substantial entities (asattvabhūta). Although there is no difference among them in having meanings that are not substantial entities, they are admitted to fall into three classes due to the restriction of their functions and the restriction of their usage. To explain: prefixes such as *pra* and others are the basis for the comprehension of the excellence of the form of an action. Particles (*nipāta*) such as the vowels and so forth are the causes for conveying the distinction between the self-nature of action and substance, having fixed forms and specific meanings.

The *karmapravacanīyas* are the causes for delimiting a relationship produced by a specific action. As it has been said: "Some divide the word (*pada*) in two ways, others in four or even five; these divisions are extracted from sentences, just like bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth. This will be explained later. A sentence (*vākya*) is of many types, because action is predominant and that [action] is unitary. As they say: "A sentence is held to have expectant parts, to consist of words that do not require further expectation toward external elements, to have action as its primary element, to possess qualifiers (*guṇa*), and to have a single meaning."

Thus, meaning (*artha*) is also of two kinds: the expressed (*vācya*) and the inferable (*anumeya*). Among these, that which is the object of the operation of the word is the expressed; it alone is called the primary (*mukhya*). As they say: "That meaning whose capacity is determined by the mere hearing [of the word] is considered the primary meaning; that which is established through effort is the secondary (*gauṇa*). Consequently, that other meaning which is inferred either from that [expressed meaning] itself or from a sign (*liṅga*) derived from it is the inferable. And that is of three types: mere matter-of-fact (*vastumātra*), poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and so forth.

Among these, the first two may also be denotable (*vācya*), while the other is necessarily inferable (*anumeya*). Among them, the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) is exclusively denotable and not inferable, because it is partless (*niraṃśa*) and lacks the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). However, the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)—insofar as parts are conceptually constructed within the denoted meaning—is to be understood as twofold, according to whether the part to be enjoined (*vidheya*) requires or does not require justification, based on its being already established or unestablished, through its status as either an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*).

In that case, regarding the established [fact], there exists a relationship between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*anuvāda*), because it is a restatement of the essential nature alone. For example: "In the northern direction, there exists the sovereign of mountains named Himālaya, the very soul of the deity; plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring rod of the earth. Here, the relationship consisting of the means and the goal (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is not yet established, because the aspect being restated is difficult to ascend to as a means. Furthermore, this relationship between the means and the goal is to be understood as being produced by the determination of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and that, in turn, must be rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that [authority] is threefold, as they say: "The world, the Veda, and likewise the inner self (adhyātma)—these are remembered as the threefold authority. Drama is for the most part established upon the subjects of the Veda and the inner self. Among these, "the world" refers to matters well-known in the world, such as: "By what means, O passionate one, were you repulsed by your angry beloved after she had prostrated herself at your feet? I shall now cause her body to experience intense remorse, making it seek refuge upon a bed of young shoots."

For here, the causal relationship between the feet and the *avadhūtī* (the central channel), as well as between the offense and the anger arising from it, is established by worldly evidence (*lokapramāṇa*), and the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is rooted therein. Or, for example: "The fickle Goddess Lakṣmī, having gone to the moon, does not enjoy the qualities of the lotus; and having resorted to the lotus, she does not enjoy the lunar splendor. But having reached Umā’s face, she attained a joy that partakes of both."

For in this case, regarding the simultaneous enjoyment of the qualities of the lotus and the splendor of the moon, the two causes—namely, the closing at night and the non-arising during the day—are already well-known in the world; thus, they do not deserve to be mentioned [as poetic figures]. A *veda* has as its object a meaning established solely by scripture. The mention of "veda" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, *dharmaśāstras*, and so forth, because these are accepted as being rooted in it. As in: "The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter when she was requested."

"A virtuous person resorts to indifference even toward a desired object out of fear of rejecting a request. For here, in the absence of the solicitation residing in the Blessed One—which serves as the cause and is based on his status as the recipient—there is the establishment of the absence of the capacity to accept the maiden, which resides in the Lord of Mountains and is the effect. This is rooted in scripture, for their relationship as cause and effect is well known to be based upon that [solicitation]. As they say: "O Bhārata, all things should be given away without being asked for!"

"Food, knowledge, compassion, and a daughter are not given to those who do not ask. Thus, the seeker is the recipient (*sampradāna*). As it has been said: "Because the agent does not reject it, the object desired by the action becomes a factor in the act of relinquishment; and through instigation or consent, it attains the status of a recipient (*sampradānatā*). And thus, this application of the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) should be understood as having a practical purpose, just as: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire. That which has the internal objects as its domain is *adhyātma*.

"Just as even Paśupati, longing for union with the Daughter of the Mountain, passed those days with difficulty—what other person under the sway of these emotions would not be overwhelmed, even that Lord whom they touch? In this passage, the causal relationship between the Lord Paśupati’s difficult passing of the days and his longing for union with the Daughter of the Mountain is established through internal logic (*adhyātmasiddha*); it is upon this foundation that the relationship of "proven" and "prover" (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between these two rests. For that [causal relationship] is of two kinds: verbal (*śābda*) and real (*ārtha*).

Furthermore, because both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) may each take the form of either a word-meaning (*padārtha*) or a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and because word-meanings are divided by the distinctions of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*), as well as by their status as property (*dharma*) or substratum (*dharmin*); and because properties themselves are further divided by the distinctions of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); and because sentence-meanings, being essentially actions, possess variety through the diversity of their factors (*kāraka*); [the syllogism] is manifold due to the various possible mutual combinations of these elements. Therefore, only a mere indication of its directions is presented here.

In that regard, when the mere quality (*dharma*) functions as the means of proof, the verbal expression (*śābda*) is as follows: "Because he disciplines, protects, and sustains his subjects, he is their father; their biological fathers are merely the causes of their birth. When that same quality is grasped in its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the sense of existence (*sattvārtha*) is as follows: "For one of great intelligence who desires prosperity, the rise of enemies is more easily endured than even a great decline, provided that decline does not tend toward the destruction of the perfection of one's fruits. Thus it is said.

For here, the relationship between the end and the means—the relation of the goal to its accomplishment—is established through the meaning of two things: the ease with which one can endure the endlessness of one who has fallen into enmity, and the difficulty with which one can endure the inclination toward the perfection of results belonging to one who has reached their destruction. However, in the absence of a relationship between a property and its substratum (dharma-dharmin), since it is merely the word-meaning itself that serves as the means, the relationship is purely verbal. As it is said: "A king perishes from bad counsel, an ascetic from attachment, a son from over-indulgence, a Brahmin from lack of study, a family from a bad son, and character from attending upon the wicked."

"Modesty [perishes] from intoxication; agriculture even from lack of supervision; affection from residing abroad; friendship from a lack of intimacy; prosperity from injustice; and wealth from generosity and negligence. Thus, even regarding the meaning of a sentence, the relationship between the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) should be understood as being of two kinds. Among these, the verbal [relationship] is, for example: "In this lake, the water of loveliness is agitated by the waves of the folds of her belly, intent on crossing the sandy banks of her hips..."

"Just as this [lake] is characterized by the movement of fish-like eyes, I think the elephant of Love—with its manifest jar-like breasts—is submerged therein. This is an example of *ārtha* (implied) indication. For example: "O friend, let this young brahmin be stopped; he wishes to say something more, for his upper lip is quivering. Not only is he who speaks ill of the great a sinner, but he who merely listens to such a person also shares in that sin. And as it is said: "If you pray for heaven, your labor is in vain; for the regions of your father are themselves the lands of the gods."

"Then, one who is fully endowed with meditative concentration does not seek out a jewel, for that [jewel] is already sought after [within him]. As for the object consisting of an inferable meaning, it is as in: "Three types of men gather the golden-flowered earth: the hero, the learned man, and he who knows how to serve. For here, in every case, the meaning is inferred—that abundant riches are easily obtained by the brave and the others—and this will be elaborated upon.

An example concerning an object that is both inferred and to be inferred is as follows: "Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this," said a friend jokingly. Having dyed her feet and offered her blessings, she struck her with a garland without a word. For here, the striking with a garland—performed by the Queen after dyeing her feet and following the friend’s joking blessing—is an *anubhāva* (consequent action) that leads one to infer the abundance of her transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), such as curiosity, eagerness, joy, and bashfulness.

And that [love], being itself inferred, leads to the inference of her passion for the Blessed Lord Bhava as her husband. As it is said: "While the celestial sage was speaking thus by her father’s side, Pārvatī, with her face cast down, counted the petals of her play-lotus. Or as in another example: "When the proud woman was offered flowers by her lover from his rival's lineage, she said nothing at all; with eyes clouded by tears, she merely traced the ground with her foot."

Just as in the case of the meaning of a sentence, where there is a clear perception of sequence between the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), so too should it be understood in the case of the object of inference consisting of a mere entity (*vastumātra*). However, in the case of rasa and the like which are to be inferred, this relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) is one of imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*); thus, the notion of simultaneity is merely an illusion. In that regard, others accept the relationship of the manifested and the manifester (*vyaṅgya-vyañjaka-bhāva*), and upon that basis, they employ the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*).

However, that [term] is employed there only in a figurative sense (*aupacārika*) and not in its primary sense (*mukhya*), because it is sublated by the principle to be stated hereafter. Furthermore, the purpose of the figurative usage is what is called "producing aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) in sentient beings. For that [wonder] is indeed observed in the case of primary objects such as paintings or statues, which are the referents of individuality. Indeed, the expressed meaning (*vācya-artha*) does not spread such aesthetic wonder as does that very same [meaning]—consisting of injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth—when it has entered into the state of being suggested through intonation (*kāku*) or being inferable (*anumeya*); this is simply the inherent nature of meanings.

For indeed, I shall not crush a hundred Kauravas in battle out of anger, nor shall I drink the blood from Duḥśāsana’s chest; I shall not shatter Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace—let the king make peace with you on such terms! Thus, having struck at our lives and our accumulated wealth through the lacquer house, the poisoned food, and the entry into the gambling hall, and having dragged away the garments and hair of the Pāṇḍava wives, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease while I yet live!

And for this reason, the perception of beauty does not arise from that which is directly expressed by its own word in the same way as it does from injunctions and prohibitions. Furthermore, two kinds of prohibition have been mentioned, based on their occurrence in the domain of nominal (subanta) and verbal (tiṅanta) suffixes. For example: "Having turned her eyes away from the King of Aṅga, the princess said to her female companion: 'It is not that he is not desirable, nor that she does not know how to see him properly; rather, people have diverse tastes. For the scope of these two types of prohibition is the negation of what was previously presumed.

And thus the author of the Dhvani says: "For the essence-nature of meaning, when manifested by not being expressed by its own word, brings forth an even greater beauty. And this is indeed a well-known fact among circles of the learned: that the most desired object is manifested as the suggested (vyaṅgya) and not as the expressed (vācya). Since the sequence of the first two [types of suggestion] is easily discernible, there is no possibility of error; therefore, the application of the term 'suggested' (vyaṅgya) in those cases is entirely without foundation.

For this very reason, the relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) cannot exist between the sounds being heard—which are designated as *dhvani*—and the object intended as *sphoṭa*, which resides within; consequently, the designation *dhvani* applied to poetry (*kāvyam*), whose nature consists of both word and meaning, based on the similarity of being a manifestor, is also untenable, because even there one must accept a relationship of the indicated and the indicator (*gamyagamakabhāva*) rooted in the causal relation of effect and cause.

But surely, it is perceived by everyone that the cognition of the mental states (*bhāva*), such as love (*rati*) and the like, arises at the very same time as the sentence-meaning consisting of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth; nor is there any awareness of an intervening obstacle such as the recollection of a relationship. Thus, the cognition of love and the like is itself the cognition of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like, and the relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is accepted in its primary sense alone. In this regard, the relationship of the signified and the signifier (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) is like that between a lamp and a jar.

As he himself has said regarding the path of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*): "When a meaning illuminates another meaning, it is perceived as the manifester of the other precisely while manifesting its own form, like a mirror. As in the verse: "While the divine sage spoke thus, Pārvatī, standing by her father’s side with her face cast down, counted the petals of her play-lotus," and so forth. Furthermore, he himself stated: "Indeed, when the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) is being perceived, the cognition of the expressed sense (*vācya*) does not disappear, because the former is manifested through its inseparable connection with the latter."

Therefore, the analogy of the jar and the lamp applies to those two. For just as when the cognition of a jar has arisen by means of a lamp, the illumination of the lamp does not cease, so too the manifestation of the expressed meaning [does not cease] upon the cognition of that which is manifested by it. It is said that the two meanings—the expressed and the implied—are cognized only successively and not simultaneously.

Just as there exists between these two the relationship of the signified and the signifier, so too has that very point been stated by the proponent of *vyakti* (manifestation) himself, who desired to define their essential nature; that same point is now written down here by us, who likewise wish to establish it. For instance: "It is certainly not the understanding of anyone that the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas* are themselves the *rasas*. Therefore, the cognition of *rasa* and the like is inseparable from the cognition of the *vibhāvas* and the rest. Since these two cognitions exist in the relation of cause and effect, a sequence is necessarily present."

However, because that sequence is not perceived due to its extreme rapidity, it has been stated that the suggested meanings, such as the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth, are indeed those whose sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*). Furthermore, therefore, just as between the denotative function and the denoted meaning, there is a sequence necessarily occurring due to the relationship of cause and effect between the cognition of the expressed and the cognition of the suggested; yet, for the reasons already stated, that sequence is sometimes perceived and sometimes not.

Thus, since the relationship of indicator (*liṅga*) and indicated (*liṅgin*) between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*) has been established according to the sequence to be explained, the inclusion of all *dhvani* within inference (*anumāna*) becomes fully justified; for it possesses a wider scope than that [inference]. Its wide scope arises because it is possible everywhere—even in domains other than *dhvani*, such as *paryāyokta* and the like, as well as in cases of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*). Furthermore, because it is preceded by the operation of speech, it should be understood as being for the sake of others (*parārtha*).

The statement that "inference for others (parārthānumāna) is the communication of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics" is not understood by the unwise world solely due to their ignorance of the aforementioned method. Now, if it is argued that every sentence-meaning necessarily contains within it the relationship between the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana), then just as there is a mandatory inclusion of both the probandum and the probans therein, so too would there be a mandatory inclusion of the example (dṛṣṭānta). This is because the example must also necessarily be required as the object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the pervasion (vyāpti); for the requirement of the example is not precluded merely by the inclusion of a probans whose capacity is already well-known. As it has been said:

For in the case of those who do not understand the example, the relation of identity (*tadbhāva*) and the relation of causality (*hetubhāva*) are both made known; however, for the learned, only the logical reason (*hetu*) itself need be stated. Now, one might ask: from what source does this arise—that the specific states of pleasure and so forth, such as love (*rati*), produce in poetry and the like a delightful aesthetic experience (*sukhāsvāda*) that charms the conscious mind, which is then postulated as the functional portion of the metaphorical designation of *rasa* and the rest as being "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*)? For in the world, when grief and other emotions are inferred from their signs (*liṅga*), not even a trace of an aesthetic experience of pleasure is observed in the inferrer.

On the contrary, it is observed that in the case of the virtuous or even the indifferent, an incomparable suffering—such as fear, grief, and dejection—arises. Nor is there any excellence in poetry or the like over the world by virtue of which [the aesthetic emotion] would be admitted only there and not in the world. For those very same worldly excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, consisting of causes, effects, and auxiliary factors, are the indicators; and those very same states such as love (*rati*) and so forth, consisting of specific conditions, are the indicated emotions (*bhāva*).

What, then, is the excellence in poetry and the like such that the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) occurs there alone and not in the world? Since the element of a purpose (*prayojana*) is absent [in the world], the metaphorical designation of *ratyādi* (love and so forth) as being "suggested" (*vyaṅgya*) is indeed untenable. It is replied: where there is the comprehension of emotional states (*bhāva*) by means of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), there alone arises the relish of aesthetic flavor, which is to be experienced solely by the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*). This is simply the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*) and does not fall within the range of objection for authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*). As Bharata said: "The production of aesthetic flavor results from the conjunction of the determinants, the consequents, and the transitory states."

As it has been said: "Rasa is said to be the meaning of poetry; it is an experience consisting of aesthetic relish, which is the domain of another's consciousness manifested by the mental states (bhāvas) and the excitants (vibhāvas). Furthermore, neither the excitants nor the mental states as such are possible in the ordinary world, because in that context only causes (hetu) and the like are found. Nor should it be thought that the excitants and the like are identical to causes and the like, for causes and the like are one thing and the excitants and the like are another, since their definitions are distinct.

For instance, those particular stable states such as love (*rati*) and others, which exist in the world as belonging to characters like Rāma, are called "emotions" (*bhāva*) when they are contemplated within oneself by poets and others for the purpose of description in poetry and the like, and thereby bring about those various aesthetic flavors (*rasas*). As Bharata said:

"Since performers bring these aesthetic moods (*rasas*) into being through various connected gestures (*abhinaya*), therefore these should be understood as *bhāvas* by those who employ dramatic art. And those causes of theirs, such as Sītā and others, when presented in poetry and other media, are called *vibhāvas* because the *bhāvas* are manifested (*vibhāvyante*) by means of them. As Bharata said: "Since many objects (*arthas*) are manifested (*vibhāvyante*) through this [means] based on vocal and physical gestures, for that reason it is designated as *vibhāva*."

Furthermore, those certain objective forms among them, such as the serenity of the face and so forth, when presented through poetry and other arts, cause those various states (bhāvas) to be experienced; thus they are called "consequents" (anubhāvas). As Bharata said: "Because an object is experienced through the representation of speech, body, and spirit, that which is joined with speech, the major limbs, and the minor limbs is known as a 'consequent'."

Furthermore, those particular transitional states that arise intermittently among them—unstable, produced by intermediate causes, and appearing in the form of surges—and which, being manifested through their respective sets of *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents), proceed with a tendency toward [the dominant] emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), are called "transitory" (*vyabhicārin*) because they move toward various such states. As Bharata said: "They are called transitory (*vyabhicārin*) because they move (*caranti*) in various ways (*vividham*) toward (*ābhimukhyena*) the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*)."

Furthermore, these forty-nine *bhāvas* that have been described—distinguished as permanent (*sthāyin*), transitory (*vyabhicārin*), and involuntary (*sāttvika*)—are all indeed transitory. The difference in their designation depends solely upon their specific, restricted forms. For instance, the status of being "permanent" is restricted to the permanent *bhāvas* alone, and not to the transitory or involuntary ones; the status of being "transitory" belongs only to the transitory *bhāvas*, and not to the other two; and the status of being "involuntary" belongs only to the involuntary *bhāvas*, and not to the other two. In this regard, there are two possible courses for the permanent *bhāvas*.

This does not apply to the transitory (vyabhicārin) and involuntary (sāttvika) states; for these are always merely transitory and are never conceived as permanent (sthāyin). As for the definition of the permanent states mentioned in the chapter on emotional states (bhāvādhyāya), it should be understood as referring only to those [transitory states] when they have reached the condition of being permanent, lest the statement of their definition be rendered purposeless. For aesthetic flavors (rasas) are held to consist of the imitation of the permanent states.

Furthermore, since their essential nature is established solely through the definition that they are "predominant" (pradhāna), and because they exist according to the analogy of the original image and its reflection, there is no inclusion of transitory states (*vyabhicārin*) among the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), such as there is for disillusionment (*nirveda*) and the like. For if they were so included, they would possess the status of stable emotions alone and not that of transitory states, just like disillusionment and the rest. Therefore, this designation of "stable emotion" even for the transitory states is employed merely on the basis of their functional suitability, in order to demonstrate the division into these three groups.

The delusion regarding the characteristics of the permanent moods (*sthāyibhāva*) in others is caused by the deception consisting merely of that [representation]; enough, then, with this digression on an irrelevant matter. Thus, since a difference in essential nature is established between the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, on the one hand, and the causes (*hetu*) and so forth, on the other—due to their being artificial or non-artificial and their being the objects of poetry or the world respectively—and since their identity is not proven, when a cognition is produced regarding the moods such as love (*rati*) and the like through the excitants and so forth, even though those [moods] are unreal, then, because they consist essentially of that [cognition], they are designated as "being perceived" (*pratīyamāna*) and "being understood" (*gamyā*).

They are indeed established in their primary sense. And it has been stated that the relish of rasa (*rasāsvāda*) consists precisely in the reflective awareness of that [aesthetic] cognition; this is its inherent nature. Or, let us set aside the idea that love (*rati*) and so forth are eternally imperceptible. For even an object that is directly perceptible does not produce such wonder for sensitive people when it is being experienced immediately as it does when it is brought within the range of a great poet’s expression. As it has been said: "The aesthetic states (*bhāva*), when presented by the power of the poet through the process of identification with them..."

"It is said that these [emotions] throb as they are presented through poetry, but not indeed in the same way when perceived through direct observation. Furthermore, even that [direct perception] does not taste as sweet to them as when it is brought to the state of being inferred by those very [poetic elements]. This is simply their inherent nature (svabhāva) and does not deserve further questioning. As it has been said: "The [emotion] inferred from the causes and other factors does not taste as sweet as when inferred from the excitants (vibhāva) and other factors; nor does the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) give pleasure in the same way as that very [meaning] when it is being realized (pratīyamāna)."

The author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has also stated: "Indeed, a meaning that is the very essence [of the work], when manifested as something not directly denotable by its own words, brings forth an even greater beauty. And since poetry and the like have as their ultimate reality mere cognition (*pratīti*), the accomplishment of the understanding of injunctions and prohibitions among those to be instructed is achieved by that alone. As it has been said: "Even an error is valid knowledge (*pramā*) by virtue of its connection [to the goal]. And: "Between one who runs toward the light of a gem and another who runs toward the light of a lamp, both thinking it to be a gem—though there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference regarding the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."

Therefore, in this context, the investigation by those with discernment into the truth or falsity of the relationship between the signifier and the signified is entirely useless. Furthermore, in a specific type of poetry (*kāvyaviśeṣa*), the investigation into the truth or falsity of the cognitions of the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) is likewise useless; thus, the examination of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein results only in ridicule. In that case, by means of causes and so forth which are themselves uncreated (*akṛtrima*), only uncreated things are made known. Since these [suggested meanings] possess only the status of being inferable (*anumeya*) and not even a trace of being suggested (*vyaṅgya*), how could there be even a trace of the savoring of aesthetic pleasure (*sukhāsvāda*) therein?

This very excellence found in poetry and other arts is established by worldly convention; thus, when rasa such as love (rati) is to be understood, the metaphorical designation of "suggested" (vyaṅgya) is justified for the purpose of experiencing aesthetic pleasure (sukhāsvāda). In its primary sense, meaning is indeed twofold: the denoted (vācya) and the understood (gamya). However, it is proven that through metaphorical usage, a third type—the suggested (vyaṅgya)—also exists. "There can never be a subordination of meaning in speech; for one takes up words for the sake of that [meaning], just as one takes up a leather bag for the sake of water. This is the summary verse (saṅgrahaśloka).

Nor can the relationship of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*) occur through the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), because the definition of manifestation (*vyakti*) is untenable. For they define manifestation as follows: it is the state of becoming an object of illumination for an existing or even a non-existing object that is being illuminated, occurring simultaneously with its illuminator, without depending on the recollection of a relation. In that regard, the manifestation of an existing thing is threefold, owing to the threefold nature of that [existing thing].

In that regard, since the effect exists within the cause in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), its manifestation (*āvirbhāva*)—characterized by the attainment of perceptibility by the senses after having been latent—is one [type of production], as in the case of curd and the like during the state of milk and so forth. However, if one does not accept such a state of existence, some call this very process "origination" (*utpatti*). The second [type of manifestation] is the appearance of that very manifested thing—which was not being perceived due to some obstruction—together with the illuminator that renders it subordinate to itself, as in the case of a jar and the like by means of a lamp and so forth.

As it has been said: "The causal efficiency of causes is established precisely through their operation; when an object is already established, that which is the cause of the cognition of another [object] through its own cognition is considered a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). And: "Whether it be a lamp or otherwise, what distinction is there between this [manifestor] and a producer (*kāraka*)? For [the manifestation] occurs from the perception resulting from the operation of all the causal factors (*karaṇa*) together. The author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has also stated: "A manifestor is defined as that which reveals another while simultaneously revealing its own nature, just as a lamp [reveals itself and] a jar, etc."

The third [type of inference] consists merely in the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding that very same previously experienced object which exists internally in the form of a mental trace, triggered by some other non-deviant entity or by something that indicates it—just as fire is inferred from smoke; or as a cow and the like are inferred from paintings, books, statues, imitations, and so forth, as well as from words. However, for a non-existent thing, there is only one such mode, since no other mode is possible—just as Indra’s bow (a rainbow) is inferred from the appearance of the sun and the world. Furthermore, this definition does not apply to the denoted object (*vācya*).

For indeed, the definition that applies to the first two meanings—namely, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of what already exists—is not capable of touching upon those things that are currently being perceived; for that would entail the consequence that they, like curd and the like, would become objects of the senses, or else, like a jar and the like, the perception of "this-ness" (*idantā*) would be impossible due to the coexistence with the denoted object. Furthermore, a definition cannot fail to touch upon the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of its subject. As for the definition of the third [meaning], however, it is consistent only with inference (*anumāna*), not with manifestation.

As it has been said: "That cognition which arises regarding the object of inference from a mark possessing the three characteristics is inference. And that is indeed inference alone. For the cognition of one thing from another thing is not possible without inference. Moreover, comparison (*upamāna*) and the other means of knowledge are included within that very [inference]. As they have said: "The conceptualization of one thing upon seeing another is not logical, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It would only be so if there were an invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*) between them. For the mere presence of something as it is established does not necessarily indicate the proximity of something else of that same kind."

Furthermore, since the comprehension of an object occurs through a general relationship, there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor can it be argued that the cognition of one object from another object is possible without the recollection of the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), for if it were so, such cognition would result for everyone at all times. Nor is there any impossibility in the definition, because—unlike the simultaneous cognitions of smoke and fire—the cognitions of those [two objects] are indeed experienced as occurring in a sequence.

If it is argued that their manifestation is intended to occur through coexistence (*sahabhāva*) in relation to rasa and so forth, then the definition suffers from the flaw of being too narrow (*avyāpti*). For there is a lack of pervasion regarding the manifestation of mere objects (*vastu*) and figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), as these do not manifest through coexistence with a manifestor. Furthermore, even in the case of rasa and the like, manifestation cannot be logically established as occurring through coexistence with the manifestation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.

For this reason, by means of those very artificial causes and so forth designated as *vibhāva* and the rest, the non-existent states such as love (*rati*)—which are like reflections and receive the designation of "permanent moods" (*sthāyibhāva*)—are brought before the path of the spectator's perception by poets; and becoming objects of relish through sympathetic resonance (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), they are called "flavors" (*rasa*). Furthermore, effects and the like cannot possibly manifest simultaneously with their causes and the like as mere reflections, because that would result in the subversion of the very determination of the relationship between cause and effect.

However, where that characteristic exists primarily [as the object itself], it is not poetry at all; so how could it possibly possess the nature of *dhvani*, which is a specific variety thereof? For the manifesting entity (*prakāśaka*) is of two kinds: that which is of the nature of an adjunct (*upādhirūpa*) and that which is independent (*svatantra*). Among these, knowledge, words, lamps, and the like are of the nature of adjuncts. As it has been said: "The three illuminators—[the mind, words, and lamps]—illuminate both themselves and others. The other is the independent kind, such as smoke and so forth.

Among these, the first [type] must certainly not be accepted by you, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that only those two objects which are denotable by words could constitute poetry. As for the other [type], it is logical only as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) and not as a suggester (*vyañjaka*), since manifestation (*vyakti*) is untenable in its case. Furthermore, even for that author Dhvani himself, the simultaneous manifestation of the threefold object intended to be suggested through the medium of the manifestor is not accepted.

As for what he says—that no one understands that the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas* are themselves the *rasas*, and that the cognition of the *rasas* and so forth arises as inseparable from the cognition of those [three factors]—since these two cognitions exist in a relationship of cause and effect, a sequence is inevitable. However, because of its extreme rapidity (*lāghava*), this sequence does not manifest; thus, the *rasas* and so forth, being suggested (*vyaṅgya*), are said to have an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*). Now, if, out of fear of this defect, this definition is stated without regard for simultaneity, even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to inference (*anumāna*).

Even in that case, there certainly exists the illumination of the object to be illuminated by means of smoke and so forth, even though the smoke itself has been made subordinate. If it is argued that this [definition] is rejected by the inclusion of the term "non-existent" (*asad*), then it would follow that the definition lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a jar and a lamp, because the jar is existent. If it is argued that the term "non-existent" will not be included, then it follows that the definition lacks pervasion in the case of sunlight and a rainbow, because the rainbow and such things are non-existent. If it is argued that neither term will be included, then the definition results in being a definition of inference (*anumāna*) alone, and not of a particular instance (*vyakti*).

That is indeed our position, because even when both the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*) exist, they manifest only in a sequential manner. Therefore, the impossibility [of your definition] remains exactly as it was, being a flaw in its definition. Furthermore, qualifying manifestation by the existence or non-existence [of the expressed] is untenable, because there is nothing to be excluded [by such a qualification]. Moreover, if that in which the expressed meaning possesses the quality of being a suggester (*vyañjaka*) is *dhvani*, then in the case of something suggested that is inferred [from the expressed], it would not be *dhvani*, because for that [inferred meaning], there is no expressed [meaning].

Furthermore, if [the definition] were stated in this manner when the celestial sage (Nārada) speaks these words, then the status of being *dhvani* would not be intended [therein], resulting in the flaw of the definition being under-extensive (*avyāpti*). Now, if both [types of meaning] are included by the word "meaning" (*artha*), since it is intended that it has both meanings as its object; as it is said: "That meaning which is praised by the connoisseurs and established as the soul of poetry—its two divisions are traditionally known as the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*)."

Granted that this is true; however, when the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the object understood through proximity as "that object" (*tam artham*), then by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), since the word "object" (*artha*) has itself been explained as referring specifically to the denoted meaning (*vācya*), it is understood to have only the denoted meaning as its scope, and not both meanings (the denoted and the indicated). Thus, the defect remains as before. Or, let us grant that it has both meanings as its scope; even so, there is the defect of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition.

If it were the case that even where the cognition of a mere fact (vastumātra) as the intended meaning is mediated by one or two other mere facts apart from the literal meaning, that too would result in being considered *dhvani*, since there is no difference in its conformity to the definition [of suggestion]. Yet, that is not accepted in such cases, because the excellence of beauty (*cārutā*) has passed away; for it is only when that [suggestion] is mediated by transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) or poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) that its status as the domain of *dhvani* is admitted. In other instances, however, the opposite is true. And in determining whether there is beauty or a lack thereof, the experts on the essence of poetry (*kāvyatattvavid*) are the authority.

In that case, there is [the figure] separated by a mere object (*vastumātra*), as in: "The hunter's wife, proud and with a peacock-feather earring, wanders amidst her co-wives who are adorned with ornaments made of pearls. Here, indeed, the superior fortune of the hunter’s wife over her co-wives is to be inferred in the manner that will be explained below.

And he was concealed by the inference that his husband was capable of killing only a peacock, due to his inability to endure the pleasure of constant enjoyment with one who had not yet renounced worldly attachments. An example of being concealed by two factors is as follows: "O merchant, where could we have elephant tusks or tiger skins? As long as the daughter-in-law with her face framed by disheveled locks moves about in the house. [In Sanskrit: *vāṇijaka hastidantā kuto 'smākaṃ vyāghrakṛttiś ca | yāval lulitālakamukhī gṛhe pariṣvakate snuṣā ||* [In English: "O merchant, whence could we have elephant tusks or tiger skins, so long as the daughter-in-law with her face adorned by dangling curls wanders about the home?"

For here, in the manner that will be explained, the elder Vyādha employs the "perception of an effect contrary to the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) in order to demonstrate the absence of elephant tusks and the like to the merchant. For example: "There is no touch of frost here, because of smoke. Indeed, the presence of elephant tusks, tiger skins, and so forth in our house is pervaded by the fact that my capable son is intent on the act of killing them.

And contrary to that [the former] is his exhaustion, produced by an incessant attachment to the pleasure of sexual union occasioned by the extraordinary good fortune of his daughter-in-law; and the effect of that is the disarray of the locks on the face of the daughter-in-law. An example of [the meaning] being mediated by three [steps] is as follows: "Seeing Brahmā at the time of inverted sexual union upon the navel-lotus, Lakṣmī, agitated with shame, kisses the right eye of Hari. [In this verse: "At the time of inverted sexual union, seeing Brahmā upon the navel-lotus..."

"Lakṣmī, overwhelmed with shame, kisses the right eye of Hari. Here, indeed, the cessation of Lakṣmī’s shame is the thing to be established. And in that regard, the cause is the kissing of the Lord Hari’s right eye, which is of the nature of the sun. For that [kissing] leads one to infer its setting, characterized by disappearance. That, in turn, through concomitance, leads to the inference of the closing of the navel-lotus. And that, again, leads to the obstruction of Brahmā’s vision. Thus, there is a realization of the inferred object mediated by three steps.

Since this succession of means is incapable of ascending to the ultimate savoring of rasa, this poetry is merely like a riddle (*prahelikā*); thus, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). An example of [rasa] not being separated by a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) is as follows: "‘Touch your husband’s head with the crescent moon,’ said a friend jokingly. Having colored her feet and offered a blessing, she struck her silently with a garland. (Kumārasambhava 3.67)

For here, in the manner described, the apprehension of the *ābhilāṣika-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of longing) regarding Gaurī is mediated by transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as curiosity, eagerness, joy, and bashfulness, which have been inferred. An example of [the apprehension of rasa] mediated by a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows: "O girl with tremulous, long eyes, since this ocean—the mass of water—does not experience even the slightest agitation now that your smiling face, filling the quarters with its beauty and luster, is before me, I consider it quite evident [that it is merely a body of water]. In this verse, the apprehension of the *vibhāva* (excitants) and *anubhāva* (consequents) of the erotic sentiment is mediated by the poetic figure of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration). This is because the statement "this is clearly a mass of water" is established through the corroboration of the fact that the ocean does not become agitated despite the proximity of a beautiful woman. Thus, the apprehension of the *śṛṅgāra-rasa* is mediated by the figure of speech. Furthermore, the apprehension of the *rasa* is not directly from the words themselves, but rather from the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas* which are suggested by those words. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of *rasa* occurs through the mediation of the *dhvani* (suggestion) of the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas*. It is not the case that there is no apprehension of *rasa* at all; rather, it is simply that the apprehension is mediated by other factors. Thus, the apprehension of *rasa* is indeed possible. Consequently, it is proven that *rasa* is the soul (*ātman*) of poetry. Therefore, the definition of poetry is: "Poetry is a sentence in which *rasa* is the soul. This concludes the discussion on the nature of *rasa*. Now, the following is stated to refute the objection that *rasa* is not the soul of poetry. This is the objection: "If *rasa* is the soul of poetry, then how can it be said that 'poetry is a sentence in which *rasa* is the soul'? For, according to the maxim "the soul is never the object of the act of knowing," the soul cannot be an object of cognition. Since *rasa* is the soul, it cannot be an object of cognition. And if it is not an object of cognition, it cannot be designated by words. Therefore, the statement "poetry is a sentence in which *rasa* is the soul" is untenable. To refute this, it is said: "The soul is not an object of cognition. This is not so. Just as the soul is perceived through inference based on the perception of its attributes (*guṇa*), so too *rasa* is perceived through inference based on the perception of its attributes. For instance, when one perceives the attributes of the soul—such as pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, cognition, and memory—one infers the existence of the soul, saying, "There must be a substratum for these qualities. Similarly, when one perceives the attributes of *rasa*—such as the expansion of the heart, horripilation, tears, and changes in voice—one infers the existence of *rasa*, saying, "There must be a substratum for these qualities. Thus, the objection that "the soul is not an object of cognition" is refuted. Furthermore, the objection that "if *rasa* is the soul of poetry, then the definition 'poetry is a sentence in which *rasa* is the soul' is untenable" is also refuted. For the soul is not the soul in the sense of being the object of the act of knowing; rather, it is called the "soul" because it is the cause of the manifestation of the self. That is to say, just as the soul is the cause of the manifestation of the self, so too *rasa* is the cause of the manifestation of the self. Therefore, the designation "soul" is applied to *rasa* by way of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*). Consequently, the definition "poetry is a sentence in which *rasa* is the soul" is perfectly tenable. Thus, the

Here too, according to the stated sequence, the relationship of the metaphorical (rūpaka) and the metaphorized (rūpya) between the face and the orb of the full moon is inferred; and the comprehension of the subject to be imitated (anukārya), which is mediated by that [inference], is precisely what must be accepted as the domain of *dhvani*, and nothing else. Nor should it be thought that this is the same in the case where there is mediation by a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) or an emotion (*vyabhicārin*), because of the lack of distinction in the mediation itself; for there is a difference in nature between a mere fact (*vastu*) and poetic figures, emotions, and so forth.

For the mere object (*vastumātra*) is of a nature entirely distinct from the inferable [object], just as smoke and the like are from fire and the like. However, [the figures such as] *vyabhicārin* and others arise conforming to its shadow, as if colored by it, as if embraced by it; they are not at all distinct from it. Thus, that "separation" (*vyavadhāna*) is something quite different from the separation of the actual object (*vastu*); therefore, that specific qualification [of the definition] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) cannot exist separately from that which is ornamented (*alaṅkārya*), because they exist in the relation of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). Consequently, the lack of distinction regarding that "separation" is likewise unestablished, and the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains exactly as before.

If "object" (artha) is intended as the meaning of the word [to be defined], that would indeed be an under-extension (avyāpti), because in such cases as "by this very speaker," there is the comprehension of one object from another object. (21)

In that case, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to both [types of poetry], since even in poetry such as riddles (prahelikā) which is separated by two or three objects, the nature of suggestion (dhvani) exists. ||22||

These are the two summary verses. However, in this very context, the general designation of the twofold nature of the meaning as the "soul of poetry" (kāvyātman) is untenable. For that [designation] is properly applicable only to the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*), since it alone—being the life-force of poetry—is intended to be the primary element as *dhvani*. As he himself has said: "The wise have traditionally declared that the soul of poetry is *dhvani*; others have denied its existence, while still others have said it is merely figurative (*bhākta*)."

"Some have said that the reality of words resides in the non-objective; therefore, we shall describe its true nature for the pleasure of the minds of connoisseurs. And: "That very meaning is the soul of poetry; likewise, in ancient times, the grief arising from the separation of the pair of Krauñca birds took the form of a verse (śloka). And: "But there is another meaning, the suggested (pratīyamāna), which exists in the speech of great poets; it shines forth as something distinct from the well-known constituent parts, like the beauty (lāvaṇya) in women."

Therefore, the reading "yaḥ kāvyasya vyavasthitaḥ" (that which is established as poetry) is appropriate in that context. Furthermore, does the word "vā" here signify an alternative (*vikalpa*) or a conjunction (*samuccaya*)? It cannot mean an alternative, because it has already been demonstrated that no other possibility exists. For example: "When his body was cast aside on the battlefield, would a dog, a crow, or the son of Drupada—his mind blinded by grief—touch his head?"

"And this foot of mine alone has been placed upon the head of that enemy—who is intoxicated by the pride of wealth consisting of countless floods of weapons—not his hand. In this case, if the plural number were intended to signify a collective (samuccaya), then where either the word or the meaning possesses suggestiveness (vyañjakatva), the status of *dhvani* would not be accepted there. Furthermore, the qualification of the word (*śabda*) would be redundant, since the understanding of it is already established by the specific nature of the meaning itself.

For this very reason, in the definition-statement, those who maintain that a work possesses the status of *dhvani* when similes (*upamā*) and the like are manifested through figures such as *dīpaka* have not included the mention of *abhidhā* (denotation), which is subordinate to itself. Otherwise, that too would have had to be mentioned, since the meaning depends upon it and figures of speech depend upon meaning; thus, both positions are untenable.

In this regard, certain self-styled scholars—whose minds are captivated by the desire to justify the use of the dual number, and who have forgotten the well-known sequence of the relationship between the signifier and the signified—perceive a simultaneity between these two, even though the expressiveness of the word has been refuted by the aforementioned reasoning. Based on that [simultaneity], they postulate a reciprocal auxiliary function between the two types of *dhvani*—namely, those where the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and those where it is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*)—with respect to the operation of suggestion (*dhvanana*), and they further construct a primary-subordinate relationship between them based on that [auxiliary function].

Since both [the word and the meaning] possess agency with respect to the act of manifestation through their cooperation, the dual number in the expression "vyaṅktaḥ" (they manifest) is used in reference to them; and considering that the alternative—whether it be the object or the word—is based on their relative predominance, they maintain that by the dual form "vyaṅktaḥ," this is what is being stated: even though in cases where the expressed meaning is not intended, the word alone is the manifestor, nevertheless the status of the meaning as a cooperative factor is not lost. Otherwise, a word whose meaning is unknown would also become a manifestor of that [meaning].

In the case of *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the intended meaning is not the literal one), the word itself certainly functions as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*), because that meaning cannot be manifested (*avyañjaka*) without being expressed by a specific word. Thus, in all instances, both word and meaning possess the function of manifestation (*dhvananavyāpāra*). Consequently, Bhaṭṭanāyaka’s refutation of the dual formulation [of the definition] is merely a "blindman's gaze" (*gajanimīlikā*). As for their claim that the alternative statement—"either the meaning or the word"—is made with the intention of referring to predominance, that is based solely on delusion and is not the truth; so enough of this insistence on a non-entity.

Furthermore, the masculine designation of the pronoun *tad* (in the word *tam*) is untenable; for that pronoun, which refers back to a previously introduced subject, must take on the gender of that very subject. Yet, no object qualified by that [masculine] gender has been introduced here, since what was immediately preceding was in fact neuter. Therefore, there exists another entirely distinct meaning perceived in that very context: "That which shines forth in the compositions of great poets, transcending its well-known constituent parts, like grace (*lāvaṇya*) in women. Thus it is said.
