One should also reverse the reading of *Sarasvatī* as "that most sweet meaning" (*svādutamam tam artham*); it is not that the very substance [of the meaning] is [different] here. For by reversing the reading in that very place, both the break in the sequence of synonyms (*paryāya-prakrama-bheda*) and the fault of the masculine designation (*puṃstva-nirdeśa*) are avoided. Here, however, there is only the single fault of the masculine designation of *tad*. And this very bed of objects of knowledge (*prameya-śayyā*) is superior.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "a particular kind of poetry" (*kāvyaviśeṣa*), the notion of poetry being "particularized" is untenable, because all poetry whatsoever is accepted as the subject of the designation *dhvani*. This is because it is admitted that poetry has rasa as its soul. As he himself said: "That very meaning is the soul of poetry; and thus, in ancient times, the grief of the first poet arising from the separation of the pair of Krauñca birds took the form of a verse. Nor can there be a "particularity" of that [rasa], because its characteristic is the savoring of unsurpassed bliss.

As they say: "When the rasa has been fully realized through recitation and then through the singing of the *dhruva* [chorus], one whose mind is solely intent on the weight of that aesthetic relish rejoices inwardly for a moment. Thereafter, when this [mind] is free from objects and established in its own true nature (*svarūpa*), its innate flow of bliss is manifested, by which yogis are satisfied. In the absence of that [rasa], even the status of being poetry would not exist for this work, let alone its specific excellence; thus, it would be something not to be undertaken by discerning people due to its fruitlessness.

For the operation of poetry, which consists in the combination of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth and is invariably concomitant with the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is called "poetry" (*kāvyam*). This is of two kinds, according to whether its subject matter is intended for performance (*abhineya*) or non-performance (*anabhineya*). In general, both types result in the fruit of providing an understanding of the domains of injunctions and prohibitions, just like a scientific treatise (*śāstra*). The distinction between poetry and dramaturgy (*nāṭya-śāstra*) is merely one of means, depending on the degree of dullness or lack of dullness in the persons to be instructed; there is no difference in their fruit.

In this regard, one [type of drama] consists merely of a description of actions that serve as the locus for well-known injunctions and prohibitions, by relying upon celebrated heroes and antagonists such as Rāma and Rāvaṇa. The other, however, consists of the direct demonstration of those very things through the process of imitation. As they say: "The description of the determinants (vibhāvas) and consequents (anubhāvas) is called poetry; but the performance of those same elements, embellished by song and so forth, is called drama."

Thus, both those of delicate intellect—such as princes and others who are averse to hearing the scriptures but live in comfort—and those who are extremely dull-witted and cannot be instructed by that much alone, being addicted to women, dancing, music, and the like, should be engaged in [the practice] by placing their desired objects before them; having given them the pleasure of tasting flavor through the "sugar-on-the-tongue" method, they should be led toward it, just as one is led to drinking bitter medicine.

Otherwise, there would be no engagement with these [poetic works] at all, much less any mastery of them. One who desires the success of the undertaking of poetry must necessarily admit that its essence is *rasa* (aesthetic flavor), because it is by being the cause of such engagement that this [poetry] exists. Furthermore, the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*) is applied solely on account of that [flavor]. Nor is it reasonable to say that when the *rasas* are distinguished, the poetry whose self is that [flavor] becomes distinguished, for such a claim lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*).

For in this way, only that which possesses a specific aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) as its very essence could be considered *dhvani* (suggestive poetry), and nothing else, because there would be an absence of distinction [from ordinary speech] in anything lacking such a flavor. Yet, it is accepted that even in those other cases [such as poetry with subordinate suggestion], this is so; thus, the definition suffers from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*). For this very reason, it cannot be said that poetry consists merely of words and meanings refined by poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), since it is only when there is the composition of the aforementioned suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) that it attains its distinctiveness. In the absence of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasātmatā*), the designation "poetry" would not apply to it in its primary sense.

How much less, then, can there be any distinction? Nor can a distinction be established for poetry, whose essence is rasa, by means of mere plot-elements (*vastu*) and the like; for these are accepted as causes for the manifestation of rasa precisely because they take the form of excitants (*vibhāva*), etc. Furthermore, it is not logical to maintain that a distinction in the manifest (*vyaṅgya*) follows from a variety in the manifestors (*vyañjaka*), just as one does not find a difference in "cowness" based on the diversity of individual cows such as *śābaleya* and others. Consequently, if one were to accept a distinction for this [rasa], the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*) would apply only to those cases where both of these [plot and sentiment] or either one of them is the thing manifested.

It is not [present] only in poetry whose soul is rasa, for there is an absence of distinction [in such cases]; yet it is desired even there, and it would also exist in insipid works such as riddles (*prahelikā*). Since even there, by the aforementioned method, it is accepted that the mere matter (*vastumātra*) and so forth are suggested (*abhivyaṅgya*), this [suggestion] is inferred as being caused solely by the nature of poetry itself through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, this must certainly be admitted even in cases such as *samāsokti* (periphrasis), and is not to be denied. Furthermore, the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna-artha*) is of only two kinds.

Since the third type, beginning with rasa, is established as being poetry itself according to the aforementioned principle, it is not proper to describe it as a subordinate member (*aṅga*), because it is intended to be the primary element (*aṅgin*). Thus, it is more appropriate to accept that the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*) refers to poetry itself, rather than to a specific variety thereof. Furthermore, when the primary form of poetry consisting of rasa is possible, it is not proper to resort to its secondary form, according to the rule: "Between the secondary and the primary, the operation [of a term] is understood to apply to the primary."

As for the designation of specific poetic genres such as the *Meghadūta* and others, that is based on the superimposition of specific intended meanings and is not primary. Thus, since the distinctiveness of poetry cannot be established [in this way], nothing would have been stated by him [Ānandavardhana] beyond what is already taught by other authorities who formulate those definitions, except for the mere designation "dhvani. Nor does even that [designation] establish anything in any way; for if its establishment were possible through that [designation], it would be unnecessary, since that [distinctiveness] is understood precisely from the connection with a specific definition that culminates in that [distinction].

Just as in the expression "the man who is mounted on a horse is the king," the man is already qualified by the horse when his relationship with that defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) occurs; it is not from that very relationship that his qualification arises. Nevertheless, this [qualification] is "unutterable" (avācya), because it is already understood through the very fact of being poetry. And since it has been stated [by others], the mention of what is unutterable is a defect. Furthermore, in the phrase "as stated by the wise," the designation of the agent of the act of stating is unutterable in both alternatives.

When there is a desire to express the agent in general, since the agent is never dissociated from the action, and when there is a desire to express a specific agent, the understanding of that specific [agent] is established precisely through the connection with a specific operation according to the sequence just mentioned; thus, to state what need not be stated is a fault.
The distinction of the meaning, the word possessing a qualifier, its gender, the dual number, the word "vā" (or), and the name "dhvani"—these constitute the excellence of poetry. ||23||
And the statement of the speaker is designated as "the characteristic of resonance" (dhvanilakṣmaṇī); thus there are ten defects.
As for those others which fall under their various subdivisions and specific characteristics, they have not been enumerated. ||24||

Thus, by excluding words corrupted by defects of definition, the meaning of the sentence defining *dhvani* remains perfectly pure: "Where a primary meaning, or a meaning inferred from it, illuminates another meaning through some kind of connection—that is called poetic inference (*kāvyānumiti*). (25)

And this is the definition of inference alone, not of anything else. As it has been said: "Inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna) is the statement of the three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅga). There is merely a difference in terminology. No one disagrees that the essence of poetry consists of its designatum, namely rasa and so forth; since that [definition] applies to the name, how could even this [definition of inference] fail to apply to it, given that there is no lack of connection with the individual instance? (26)
The word has but a single power, namely denotation, and the object has but a single status, namely being a logical mark;
it has been established that neither of these possesses the capacity for suggestion. ||27||
It has been stated that the inclusion of the word "sound" (śabda) in the definition of suggestion (dhvani) is entirely redundant;
for there is no instance accepted by the learned authorities where it leads to a different meaning [in this context]. (28)

Nor is it appropriate for those two [the word and its meaning] to be qualified by being subordinate (upasarjana), because even in poetry where the suggested sense is subordinated (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), beauty is indeed desired. ||29||
For this very reason, even the employment of a qualifier is not purposeful;
it is understood that its sole fruit is the mere establishment of a connection with a name. (30)

In that case, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding the name, because it would apply to any other specific quality whatsoever contained within the sentence due to its attainment [of that status]. (31)
Therefore, that in which an implied meaning appears—whether clearly, predominantly, or otherwise—through the power of the expressed meaning, is called poetry. (32)
Between the expressed and the implied meanings, there exists no relationship of the manifestor and the manifested;
for, unlike a lamp and a jar, those two do not manifest one another through coexistence. (33)

Because it depends upon the establishment of the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), the relation, and the pervasion (vyāpti)—just as in the case of "tree-ness" and "mango-ness," or as in the case of "fire" and "smoke. (34)

In this case, it is logical that [the cognition] is indeed inferential, because it conforms to the definition of inference. Furthermore, regarding non-existent things such as Indra’s bow (a rainbow), what could its manifestation be? It is simply a mental construction. (35)
For while being an effect is admitted even for that which is non-existent, its being a cause is contradicted;
because it lacks all causal capacity, like a sky-lotus and the like. (36)
The employment of words is generally utilized for the sake of others; for without it, one is unable to bring another to an understanding. (37)
Furthermore, no one would either engage in or desist from action based on a reason that is devoid of expectation;
therefore, it is intended that such a reason must contain within itself both the goal to be accomplished and the means thereto. (38)
Each of these two is to be known as twofold, through the distinction between being verbal and being objective;
those two are also considered to be twofold, by way of being the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence. (39)

In that regard, the objects to be established are threefold: the mere thing (vastumātra), the poetic figures (alaṅkāra), and the aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and so forth. Among these, the first two are the domain of verbal testimony and inference. (40)
The final [element] is the object of inference; however, it is called "suggested" (vyaṅgya) by virtue of its figurative application (bhakti).
That aspect of the purpose of this figurative application which consists of the quality of aesthetic wonder (camatkāritva) [is what constitutes suggestion]. 41.
Since that [sentiment] exists therein, it too has its single cause in the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth;
for this very reason, the consequence of [an excess of] aesthetic wonder (camatkāra) does not follow even in the world. ||42||
In that regard, the causes and so forth exist, but not the manifestations and so forth;
therefore, one should not suspect these to have the same referent, because their defining characteristics are distinct. (43)
And this is the very nature of objects that they do not please directly in their own form, but do so once they have come within the range of the words of a great poet. (44)

These are the summary verses. Furthermore, as for the postulation of a separate operation on the grounds that this [word] is the substratum of multiple powers, that applies only to the object and not to the word, because it is unestablished that the word is the substratum of multiple powers. For indeed, powers residing in a single substratum are observed to produce their respective effects simultaneously—having independent functions and lacking any natural restriction of sequence—just as, for example, the powers of burning and illuminating belong to fire.

Furthermore, powers (śakti) that have sound as their substratum are neither observed nor accepted as functioning invariably preceded by the power of denotation (abhidhā-śakti), because we observe the operation of other powers [such as inference] based on that very [denotative power]. Therefore, it must be understood that these [other powers] have distinct substrata and do not have sound alone as their sole substratum. And since that distinct substratum is the object (artha) itself, one must necessarily accept that its function is included within inference.

For instance, in cases such as "The Vāhīka is a cow," the referents such as "cow" have their own meanings sublated by the other meaning, the Vāhīka; yet, because the prescription of identity with that [Vāhīka] would otherwise be inexplicable, they lead one to infer its reality there through some particular aspect, but not in its entirety.

For no one who is not insane would, upon failing to perceive some similarity in any way whatsoever, suddenly superimpose reality [upon it]. A cognizer who has familiarized himself with the nature of the speaker must understand that the mere similarity is the cause for the superimposition of reality, and not reality itself. For that [reality] appears only at the outset as something to be expressed; it cannot be the locus where the cognition culminates, because its sublation is possible.

The cause for such an application is the demonstration of mere similarity; and the purpose is the demonstration, with brevity, of qualities such as dullness belonging to cows and the like in [people] such as the Vāhīkas. For this method of extended application (atideśa) is what is called "the application of a word to another object. As it has been said: "Others know that as secondary (gauṇa), where a class-word is employed even in the absence of the class itself, on account of a quality similar to that which belongs to the related [primary object]."

"Thus, this bed of lotus leaves—withered on both sides due to contact with her full breasts and hips, yet failing to reach the middle of her body because of its narrowness; disarrayed by the tossing and turning of her limp vine-like arms—speaks of the fever of the slender-limbed woman. This is how it should be understood in such cases. For the definition of inference has been stated as "the cognition of one thing from another, preceded by the determination of an inseparable relation (avinābhāva)," and that very definition is indeed found here.

For instance, in such cases as "he speaks" (*vadati*), there is the cognition of another meaning, namely "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) and so forth. And the invariable concomitance between these two is established by the relation of cause and effect, since it is well known that manifestation is the effect of speaking. Nor can it be said that "manifestation" is the primary denotation (*vācya*) of the root *vad*, because that [meaning] is not conventionally associated with it, and because "manifestation" is not its actual referent. Furthermore, this [word] does not convey its own literal meaning alone, for that would result in a contradiction.

Now, if it is argued that the verb *vadati* (he speaks) refers to another action called "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) which is similar to the act of speaking—on the grounds that the act of speaking itself cannot otherwise be accounted for as a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*)—then it follows that manifestation and so forth, being perceived through the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of speaking and the like, must be merely inferable. This is because it has been accepted that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference (*anumāna*).

Therefore, this cognition of similarity between a person from the Vāhīka region and a cow, which is constructed on the basis of the "otherwise-unaccountability" of superimposing [the nature of] that [cow] upon him, is the object of inference alone, and not of the operation of the word; thus it is established.
Or rather, by the superimposition of "cowness" upon the Vāhīka, his similarity to it is inferred;
for what wise person would designate something as being that very thing which is not similar to it? (45)

This is the summary verse. Even in cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," meanings such as the Gaṅgā—whose status as the locus of the hamlet is sublated by their own inherent impossibility of being so—lead, through the force of their being the basis [of the usage], to the inference of another object in the form of the bank and so forth. This other object is capable of assuming the status of that locus because its true nature is metaphorically superimposed upon it based merely on a relationship [with the Gaṅgā]. For it is not accepted that similarity alone is the sole basis for the superimposition of a true nature.

Rather, since that [connection] and so forth also exist, it must be the bank and such—which has the nature of being "that" (the river) superimposed merely through its connection with it—that is the object of inference for the referents such as the Ganges, because otherwise the status of being the locus of the hamlet and so forth would be inexplicable. On the other hand, the word, having its capacity exhausted by the mere operation of denoting its own primary meaning, does not even venture to know anything of another object such as the bank, let alone come into contact with it; thus it has been said.

Furthermore, the purpose of this employment of such a variety of expressions is the comprehension of qualities—such as holiness and coolness—belonging to the Ganges and so forth, which are superimposed upon the object that serves as the locus of superimposition, such as a riverbank; it is not similarity [that is intended]. This is its distinction from the former [type of metaphor]. In both cases, however, the cause is precisely the superimposition of identity (*tattvāropa*). For that [superimposition] is held to be manifold, being based on similarity to that [object], connection with that, and so forth. As they say: "Through proximity to the denoted object, through similarity, or through inherence..."

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is considered to be fivefold due to the reversal [of the primary meaning] and the application of function. Furthermore, since the rule of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with those [secondary meanings] is established through worldly usage alone, there is no need for the exertion of seeking another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein. For it is observed that people in the world employ a term for an object similar to it or for something connected to it as being the thing itself; for example, seeing someone with a long neck and a large body, one designates him a "camel" (*karabha*), or referring to some people on a platform who are shouting, one says, "the platforms are shouting."

Furthermore, in the case of figurative usage (*upacāra-vṛtti*), some basis must necessarily be followed so that there may be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the word. Otherwise, how could a word whose relationship is well-established elsewhere convey a completely different meaning? And that which serves as its basis is precisely what we have designated here as the "mark" (*liṅga*). This is logical, because the word has no operation (*vyāpāra*) upon that [new meaning], and its lack of operation follows from the absence of a relationship.

Since the cognition of the possessor of a mark (liṅgin) from the mark (liṅga) is nothing other than inference, the cognition of another meaning [the secondary sense] through the function of quality (guṇavṛtti) is not verbal; thus, its status as being based on a denotative word is unestablished.

That superimposition of identity which is based upon a connection [between the primary and secondary senses], when there is a sublation of the primary meaning, would likewise lead to the inference of a [non-verbal] connection. (46)
For similarity to that [object] and connection with it are the sole causes for the superimposition of its true nature;
since the cognition of that [nature] arises from the two-fold figurative function (guṇavṛtti), it is therefore an inference. 47.
The abandonment of the primary function of a word is not tenable;
for a meaning prescribed in another sense would lead one to infer its similarity to its own [primary] meaning. (48)
For in the case of objects such as "equal" and so forth, people superimpose a meaning remembered from seeing that [object];
but a word does not [do so] for those who follow only its own primary meaning. 49.
Thus, since the application of the word to any other referent is untenable, how could the word have a faltering application when the result is to be known solely through its inferential mark? (50)
The primary function (mukhyā vṛtti) of the word-sound (dhvani) is declared to be direct with respect to its own operation;
however, this [secondary function] follows from the superimposition of a meaning and is figurative (gauṇī) due to that intervention. (51)

Because it is not perceived as impure, the world does not apprehend the superimposition of meaning [upon the word] without first apprehending the superimposition of the word—as in cases such as "cow" or "Caitra. (52)
Because the object and the word exist in a relationship of primary and secondary status, their simultaneous attribution as equals is not tenable. (53)
Where a distinction is perceived regarding the object of superimposition, that is cited as figurative usage (guṇavṛtti) based on the superimposed meaning. ||54||

To the extent that the totality of causes (sāmagrī) is desired as the basis for the figurative application of words, that very same [totality] is accepted by us as the indicative mark (liṅga) with respect to another object. (55)
For that [object] cannot be considered the denotable meaning of a word due to the absence of a convention;
moreover, since it is being apprehended, its nature as an inferable object is evident. (56)
Therefore, words have no movement toward another object beyond their own primary meaning;
consequently, there is no possibility of figurative usage (guṇavṛtti) based on denotative power (vācakatva). ||57||
And through its devotion [to the primary meaning], this *dhvani* maintains oneness with it despite differences in form;
nor is it not characterized by that [devotion], because of the absence of both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). (58)
In the verse beginning with "suvarṇapuṣpām" and others, the charge of non-pervasion (avyāpti) does not apply;
for figurative usage (bhakti) is said to be twofold, based on the distinction between the meaning of a word and the meaning of a sentence. ||59||
The superimposition of that [quality] upon what is not that is held to be the defining characteristic of *bhakti*;
this mode is also praised as being for the purpose of conveying another meaning. (60)
Furthermore,
those words such as "lāvaṇya" (beauty) which have become conventionalized in another sense— even if they also apply to their own primary sense— are not applicable as instances of *dhvani*. (61)
The meaning is that they certainly do exist. For:

"When the perception of an object occurs through a secondary function (guṇavṛtti) by abandoning the primary function (mukhyā vṛtti), the word does not falter in its course toward that very result for which it was intended. (62)
Why should the function of suggestion (guṇavṛtti), which is based solely on the power of denotation, not be the domain of Dhvani, whose sole root is the capacity to suggest? 63.
Furthermore, the claim that suggestion (dhvani) has as its sole basis the quality of being a manifestor is unproven;
for even the secondary function (guṇavṛtti) is accepted as depending on the capacity of being a signifier, and it is upon that [capacity] that [suggestion] relies.

Words such as *samit* and *idhma*, which are well-known as functioning through metaphorical indication (*guṇavṛtti*), have been employed as examples for sound (*dhvani*) that is manifested by words and the like. (65)

Therefore, even that usage of a word which, due to a lack of proficiency or expressive power, proceeds with faltering movement, should be understood as having inference as its object, just like any other [usage]. (66)

These are the summary verses. Even in such cases as "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house," this apparent permission to eat poison—assisted by the context and other factors—inferentially indicates that eating in that person's house has a consequence even more terrible than that.

For a person who understands the nature of the speaker, the context, and so forth—knowing that one who is not insane, being desirous of the welfare of a friend and the like, would not suddenly permit the eating of poison while otherwise prohibiting food at a certain place—is entitled to infer from that very permission to eat poison that dining at that person's house is absolutely not to be done.

For the presentation of the sentence-meaning—such as the permission to consume poison—which is itself irrelevant (aprastuta), must be understood as a cause (*hetu*) in that context, since it aims at conveying another matter distinct from the relevant topic (*prastuta*), according to the principle stated previously; thus, no further function of the word need be postulated there. Those who know the context and the nature of the speaker infer from this expressed meaning (*vācya*) the extreme cruelty of eating food in this house, which exceeds even the consumption of poison. (67)
For no wise person would ever, without cause, approve of the consumption of poison by a friend;
therefore, in this case, the comprehension of another meaning arises from the power of intention (*tātparya-śakti*), and not otherwise. (68)

This is for the sake of summary. Furthermore, others do not believe that there is a single, very long operation of the word—like a single arrow—that begins with the comprehension of the expressed meaning and culminates in the apprehension of another implied meaning; rather, they maintain that no separate [cognition] of another meaning is perceived at all. For just as a single arrow released by a powerful archer pierces both the armor and the chest of the enemy and takes away his life, [so too is the operation of the word].

Nor does it possess a difference in its mode of operation; likewise, a word uttered once by a skilled poet expands both the expression of its own primary meaning and the cognition of another meaning through a single activity, and there is no distinction whatsoever in its function. Furthermore, according to the principle that "the purpose for which a word is used is its meaning," it is logical that this [secondary] function belongs to the word itself and not to the meaning. This is incorrect, because it is not established that the word is the direct cause of the cognition of the meaning.

If, however, its causality is accepted only in a mediated sense, then the rule governing the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect among entities would not be established. Consequently, even a potter, while fashioning a jar that serves as an instrument for irrigation water, might be primarily designated as the cause of the blossoming of flowers—as if it were the month of spring. Therefore, it is logical to accept that the operation belongs to the object itself, and not to the word.

For it cannot be said in a primary sense that whatever operation belongs to the son belongs to the father alone, because that would entail the fault of confusing the respective operations of the two. Furthermore, this presentation of the arrow as an analogy is flawed; for a word does not function in the same way as an arrow, which by its very nature performs various effects—such as cutting or piercing—upon objects like those to be cut or pierced through a single mode of action.

For that [word] initiates its own operation depending upon convention (*saṃketa*), and not by its very nature; thus, it operates only where its convention exists. Consequently, it is logical that its operation has as its object only the denotable meaning (*abhidheyārtha*), and not another object, because there is no convention regarding the latter. Even if one were to imagine such an operation toward that other object despite the absence of convention, everyone would perceive that other object from some [word], just like the denotable meaning itself.

Therefore, it is logical to understand that its function operates only where there is a dependence on convention (saṅketa), and not with respect to another object, because in that case, as will be explained later, the establishment of the object's suitability is accomplished by the object itself. Furthermore: "Word and meaning, joined together and established within a composition characterized by the skillful operation of a poet, constitute poetry which brings delight to those who know it."

Some who consider themselves connoisseurs of aesthetic taste (*sahṛdaya*) declare that the very life of poetry is a quality called *vakratā* (curvature or deviation), characterized solely by a variety of expression that differs from the conventional usage of words and meanings established in the scriptures and other such sources; however, this too is incorrect.

For this deviation from the established connection between word and meaning would either result merely in a lack of propriety (*aucitya*) regarding them, or it would be intended to manifest a suggested sense (*pratīyamāna*) that deviates from the well-known denotative meaning; since no other mode is possible for the variety of the composition of words and meanings that transcends the established tradition. Of these, the first alternative is not even worth considering, because its distinct employment possesses a variety that is established by the very capacity required for defining the nature of poetry.

For the function of the poet consists solely in the composition of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, and nothing else. And these, when composed in accordance with the treatises, serve as the basis for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), but not otherwise. Since poetry has aesthetic flavor as its very soul, how could contact with impropriety (*anaucitya*) be even conceivable therein, such that those who consider themselves wise would propound a definition of poetry in this manner for the purpose of excluding it?

If, however, the second alternative is accepted, then this definition of *dhvani* would merely be stated in a different manner, because the entity [of *dhvani*] is non-different [from what has already been defined]. For this very reason, its divisions and those same examples shown by them [would be redundant]. That this is improper has already been stated and will be further explained.

"That meaning which, having abandoned the well-known path, is expressed in an entirely different way for the sake of achieving artistic variety (*vaicitrya*), is cited as *vakrokti* (oblique expression). (69)
Since that meaning is understood through words, sentences, and so forth, it is considered to be manifold;
therefore, those who know [the subject] maintain that its "curvature" (vakratā) is likewise desired to be manifold. (70)

To this it is replied: In the manifestation of meaning by a word, only one operation is accepted, namely that which is designated as "denotation" (abhidhā); everything else belongs to the meaning itself. (71)

If the meaning [suggested] is distinct from the expressed meaning, then that [expressed meaning] is its indicator (liṅga); for its definition is its connection through invariable concomitance (tannāntarīyakatayā). ||72||
If there were no difference [between the literal and the suggested], the expression would not occur in manifold ways, because one would not grasp another path [of meaning] through that statement.
Therefore, just like *dhvani*, why should this *vakrokti* (oblique speech) not also be considered inference (*anumā*)? 73.

These are the intermediate verses. Nor is it logical for a word to possess a distinct function of manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) apart from its denotative function (*abhidhā*), by which it might convey another meaning; for such a manifestation is untenable, and no other relation [between the word and that meaning] is established. Even if one were to admit such a function despite its absence, there would be no restriction regarding its specific meaning, as there would be no basis for it. For this [function of manifestation] does not have an inherent relation with the emotional states (*bhāva*) such as love (*rati*) and so forth, in the same way that a song has an inherent relation with its melodies; otherwise, everyone would necessarily perceive those emotions.

Nor is it produced by convention (*samaya*), because the capacity to manifest [meaning] is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and since the adventitious conditions—consisting of the collection of factors such as the intended meaning and the context—are infinite and indeterminate, it is impossible to establish a convention for every single word, just as it is impossible to provide a grammatical instruction for every single word. Indeed, a single word alone conveys various distinct meanings through the diversity of its capacities. As it is said: "The sky is smeared with the luster of glossy, dark clouds; the clouds are accompanied by cranes darting about; the winds are laden with droplets; and the sweet, joyous cries of the peacocks, the friends of the clouds, resound."

"Granted that Rāma is firm and hard-hearted, and that I am he who endures everything; but how will Vaidehī fare? Alas! Alas! O Queen, be steadfast! "The cruel Rākṣasa did what was fitting for one enraged by her rejection; she endured it, and you, too, have endured it, such that the people of noble lineage now hold their heads high. But now, O beloved, Rāma—who bears this bow in vain as a witness to your calamity, and who prizes his own life—has done what is unbecoming of love."

"O Right-Handed One! Release your sword from this Śūdra ascetic for the sake of the life of the deceased brahmin boy. You are the hand of Rāma, skilled in the exile of Sītā when she was distressed by her heavy pregnancy; whence can there be compassion for you? Having remembered this, come now, O Lord! Having seen Sagara and Bhagīratha, and having seen my bow and my arrows while Rāma dwelt on the riverbank and lay upon a bed of Kuśa grass—even today, O Blessed One, there is no regard for you [from me]. In such passages, the word *rāma* occurs only once.

As the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has said: "The function characterized by suggestiveness (*gamakatva*), which conforms precisely to that well-known relationship between word and meaning called the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*), proceeds as a contingent (*aupādhika*) operation due to the presence of other auxiliary factors. For this very reason, it is distinct from the denotative power (*vācakatva*). Denotative power is indeed the fixed nature of a specific word, established through its inseparable connection with its meaning from the time of the learning of convention (*saṅketa-vyutpatti*)."

However, that [inference] is non-definitive because it is conditional (*aupādhika*); for, through the delimitation of context and so forth, its nature is perceived otherwise. Furthermore, since no other relation between these two [the word and the object] is possible, it is established that the capacity to indicate that [object] belongs to that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone by virtue of the power of the relation, and not to the word itself. Thus, there is no distinction between this [position] and the position regarding the object; therefore, the presentation of that [word-based] position is useless.

Now, if it is not accepted that a word has the capacity to manifest meaning independently of its referent, then how is it that in examples such as *prāpta*, the prefix *pra* and others are said to be "illuminators" (*dyotaka*) and not "denoters" (*vācaka*)? For if they were denoters, since the verbal root would begin with a consonant (*hal*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of the *yaṅ* suffix and so forth. Is it not the case that "being an illuminator," "being a manifester," and "being a suggester" are one and the same thing? True; this was stated figuratively and not in an ultimate sense, because the actual property residing in things like lamps—which consists in being a subject of both word and meaning—is rejected [in the case of prefixes].

Now it is said: verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks) express general action (*kriyāsāmānya*). And since generalities encompass all their particular instances (*viśeṣa*), the existence of those particulars is established by the very fact that they are invariably concomitant with the cognition of that generality. As they say: "A generality devoid of particulars would be like the horn of a hare. Thus, although the [particulars] are established by the force of the object itself (*arthasāmarthya*), they require a manifestation (*dyotana*). Therefore, prefixes (*prādi*) and the like, whose function consists solely of that [manifestation], must be regarded as indicators (*dyotaka*) alone, not as denoters (*vācaka*).

True; however, that which does not result in the cognition of a universal when it itself is not cognized—let that mere particular indeed be understood from those [words]. But no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is established by that much alone, because such usage is dependent upon the determination of a specific, fixed particular. That [universal], arising for the first time from *pra* and so forth, is perceived; it is not [perceived] from *pacati* and so forth, nor is its existence established even from the meaning (*artha*), because this [usage] is dependent upon the determination of a specific, fixed particular.

Therefore, it is logical to accept that the relationship between the denoted and the denoter applies only to those two things whose cognition follows the presence and absence of the employment [of a word], and not to their being objects of manifestation; as is the case with the word "jar" and its referent. Since in cases such as "he cooks," the cognition of excellence and so forth follows the employment of prefixes and the like, they too must necessarily be of that same nature.

Otherwise, in the case of the "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and similar expressions, the conventional usage of the relationship between qualifier and qualified—between every word intended as a qualifier such as "blue" and the word denoting the particular such as "lotus"—would come to an end. For even in that case, it could be argued that words such as "lotus" denote universals (*sāmānya*).

Since universals (sāmānya) contain particulars within them, once their existence therein is established, words such as "blue" and so forth must also function merely as indicators (dyotaka) of those [particulars], like the particle *pra* and others, and not as denoters (abhidhāyaka). Furthermore, in this way, since jars and the like would have their existence established by revolving only within the internal [cognition], even words such as "jar" would be mere indicators and not denoters; thus, the linguistic convention of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācaka-vyavahāra*) would come to an end.

Therefore, one must accept that the capacity to illuminate is merely figurative (*bhākta*) and not primary. And the purpose of this figurative usage is the clear apprehension of the expressed meaning. As for the cause [of this figurative usage], it is the perception of simultaneity due to the non-perception of sequence, because the cognition of the qualifier and the specific [qualified] object occurs with such rapidity. For a qualifier is held to be of two kinds: internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*). Among these, the former effects its purpose immediately, like lac dye on crystal and the like.

The second type is of both forms, like a magnet with respect to iron. For that [magnet] indeed imparts its own power to the iron even when it is separated by a distance. That too is twofold: having the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) and having different loci (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is also twofold: the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the meaning of a nominal stem (*nāmārtha*). Among these, the domain of prepositions (*upasarga*) is generally the meaning of a verbal root, not the meaning of a nominal stem; however, for particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca* and others, it is both.

It should be understood that the rule regarding their sequential application—first the qualifier and then the qualificand—applies strictly to those [two] alone, and not to other qualifiers. Thus, when the nature of the qualifier and the qualified has been established, that which is called the "internal" qualifier is, as it were, included within the very nature of the qualified, like "cowness" (gotva) in the case of a cow; because the cognitions of these two occur so rapidly, no sequence is perceived, and the resulting impression of simultaneity is the cause of the delusion regarding the relationship between the illuminator and the illuminated.

For this very reason, some—considering these [particles] as if they were included within the verbal roots (*dhātu*)—have stated such things as: "The separate conceptualization of *aṭ* and the other [augmentative particles] is for the sake of establishing their specific application; however, in the grammatical treatise, between the root and the prefix, the root alone is of such a nature. Furthermore, there is no interval at all between particles such as *ca* (and) and the clear substrates that serve as their qualificands, just as there is none between lac-dye and crystal stones. Therefore, whatever [qualificandum] is immediately conditioned by them, those particles are capable of imparting a specific quality to that very thing and to nothing else.

As for their occasional occurrence in a different order, that is simply untenable; for if those [words] were placed out of their proper position, they would—by their own coloring—color an unintended different meaning. Consequently, there would arise the undesirable consequence of inconsistency in the matter at hand.

If, by some means, one were to attempt to establish a connection with the intended meaning despite a displaced word order (*bhinnakrama*), the comprehension of the subject at hand would be obstructed; consequently, the savoring of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) based upon that [comprehension] would also be obstructed. This is because verbal defects are admitted to be a form of impropriety (*anaucitya*), and such impropriety is a cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor. As they say: "There is no cause for the disruption of aesthetic flavor other than impropriety; indeed, adherence to well-known propriety is the supreme secret (*upaniṣad*) of aesthetic flavor.
The capacity of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry) to manifest [meaning] is not natural (*svābhāvika*) like a lamp;
rather, it is artificial (*kṛtaka*) like smoke, as it depends upon [factors such as] the relationship between words and meanings. (74)

The view held by some that particles such as *pra* possess the quality of illumination (*dyotakatva*) is accepted by them only in a figurative sense; it is not primary, because that [primary sense] is impossible in their case. ||75||
For it is thus: that object whose cognition follows the presence or absence of a particular word is said to be the denoted meaning of that word. (76)
Just as the meaning of the word "cow" is "cow," that [meaning] would otherwise be indeterminate;
furthermore, there would be no conventional usage regarding the denotability of any object whatsoever. (77)
Since the cognition [of the word] follows the sequence of the application of the prefix, the root, and the suffix, why should that [word] not be denotative of excellence and so forth? (78)
Because there is no apprehension of distinction and because the sequence is not perceived, the simultaneous occurrence [of the two] is an error that serves as the basis for devotion. //79//
The qualifier, moreover, is of two kinds: internal and external.
Among these, that which is immediate and effective toward its object is internal. (80)
Like lac on crystal, the second [kind of contact] is of a dual nature;
like iron and its magnet, that too is considered to be of two kinds. (81)

The qualificand (viśeṣya) is also to be known as twofold, based on the distinction between having a non-identical or identical substratum (asamāna-samānādhikaraṇatva), and based on the distinction between the meanings of verbal roots (dhātu) and nominal stems (nāman). ||82||
The meaning of a noun is also considered to be twofold, by way of the distinction between being verbal and being objective.
Among these, the meaning of a verbal root is generally held to be the domain of prefixes (upasargas). (83)
Regarding particles such as "ca" (and) and others, both [positions] have been proclaimed;
however, they may occur either solely before or after the qualified object, according to the sequence. 84.
The sequence of other qualifiers is unrestricted;
such being the nature of this relationship between the qualifier and the qualified. (85)
That internal qualifier which has been described as having a dual nature remains as if submerged in the qualificand, like "cowness" residing in a cow. (86)
Precisely because they are not perceived as distinct, there is no apprehension of a sequence between the two;
and this is the very root of the delusion regarding their relationship as the illuminated and the illuminator. (87)

Furthermore, because [the author] accepted that *pra* and the other prefixes contain verbal roots within them, the best among the learned stated: "The rule for the placement of *aṭ* and the others is for the sake of systematic arrangement," and so forth. (88)

For this very reason, the wise do not accept a connection with particles such as *ca* when they are separated [by other words], because those particles would impose their own power upon what is immediately adjacent. (89)
But if there were an interval, these [words] would place that capacity in something else entirely;
consequently, due to the inconsistency of the meaning, an impropriety would result. (90)
That [non-apprehension] is considered to be of two kinds, distinguished by being external (bahiranga) or internal (antaranga).
Among these, that which has exclusively words as its object is declared to be external. (91)
That second [type], which has objects as its domain, has already been demonstrated by the predecessors themselves;
therefore, its specific nature will not be elaborated upon here by us. (92)
This very thing is understood both indirectly and directly as a cause for the disruption of rasa in the case of a poet who is not vigilant. (93)
As for this [fault] concerning words which is observed in many ways, its five origins are the defects arising from a deviation in the initial undertaking (prakrama). ||94||
We shall describe their essential nature in brief; as for the detailed elaboration of these five, one should understand it oneself. (95)

These are the summary verses. Furthermore, one who desires to explain the true nature of poetry (*kāvya*) must first state its general definition; for once it is established that "poetry is that wherein there exists a relationship of signifier and signified between the expressed (*vācya*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*)," the purpose of the explanation is accomplished by that much alone. As for the two-fold division stated without such a definition—by positing the status of primary and secondary between those two—that is entirely irrelevant.

For that alone which is determined to be the cause for the cognition of a particular attribute becomes what is to be communicated to one who seeks that attribute, and nothing else, because of the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For example, in the cognition of "the man with the staff" (*daṇḍin*), it is the staff [that is the cause]. And it has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the mere contact with the object to be inferred is the cause of the beauty of poetry. Therefore, only that [contact] needs to be stated; there is no distinction here based on whether it is primary or secondary.

Indeed, in all three types of inferable objects—namely, the mere thing (*vastumātra*), the quality (*guṇa*), and the action (*kriyā*)—no specific distinction is perceived that evokes a particular aesthetic charm (*cetana-camatkāra*). Among these, when the mere thing is predominant, as for example: *vacca maha vvia ekkāe hontu ṇīsāsaroīavvāim | mā tujjha vi tīe viṇa dakkhiṇṇahaassa jāandu ||* "Let sighs and weeping belong to me alone; let them not arise even for you, who are struck by courtesy, in the absence of her. [In Sanskrit: *vrajantu mamaivaikasyā bhavantu niśvāsaroditavyāni | mā tavāpi tayā vinā dākṣiṇyahatasya janiṣata ||* "Let [these] proceed from me alone; let them be mine only. Let them not be born even for you, who are overcome by courtesy, in the absence of her."

When that very [object] is not predominant, as in: "What indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon; wherein the temples of elephants emerge, and wherein there are other stalks of plantain and lotus fibers? And as in: "The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its precursor; oh, how strange is the course of fate, yet even so there is no union."

An example of the predominance of ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows: "The gaze of heroes delights not so much upon the breast of their beloved, red with saffron, as it does upon the frontal globes of their enemies' elephants, thick with vermilion. And likewise: "Their hearts are of a single flavor toward that ornament which is the kinsman of the *śirīṣa* flower."

"The flower-arrowed god has fixed his beloveds' bimba-like lips as the target. Thus, their hearts, which find a single flavor in seizing jewels that are siblings to the goddess Śrī, have been fixed by the flower-arrowed god upon the bimba-like lips of their beloveds. This is the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā* (The Play of the Odd Arrow). As for its subordination (*aprādhānya*), it is as follows: "By the moon, the night; by lotuses, the night-lily; by clusters of flowers, the creeper; by swans, the beauty of autumn; by good people, the story of poetry is made weighty. This is the *Candamaūha*.

"The night is made weighty by the moonbeams, the lotus-pond by its lotuses, the creeper by clusters of blossoms, the autumnal splendor by swans, and poetic narrative by virtuous men. Regarding the predominance of rasa and the other elements, examples are found in the *Kumārasambhava* during the episode of Madhu: in the description of the Goddess’s arrival while wearing ornaments of spring flowers, up to the point of the fixing of the arrow by Manobhava (the God of Love), and in the description of the specific gestures of Śambhu as his fortitude was revealed.

Their subordination (*aprādhānyam*) is of two kinds, based on the distinction between being pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*). Among these, the pure is as follows: "Of what use is laughter? Will you not come back again? It has been a long time since we last met. O heartless one, why this fondness for exile? By whom have you been driven far away? Speaking thus in their dreams, with their necks clasped by their beloveds, the women of the enemy host wake up and weep loudly, their armlets empty upon their bare arms. In this instance, the pure *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment alone functions as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).

"As when he was thrown off by the young women of Tripura as their hand was grasped, who seized the hem of her garment even as she struck him violently, who was cast away as he took hold of her hair, who was not looked upon with agitation as he fell at her feet, and who was shaken off even as he embraced her—may that fire of Śambhu’s arrow, like a lover whose offense is fresh, burn away your sins, he before whom the young women stood with eyes like blue lotuses wet with tears. Thus it is said.

For here, since the excellence of the power of the Enemy of Tripura constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) characterized by jealousy becomes a subordinate element (*aṅga*) precisely through its association with *śleṣa* (punning). Thus, it should be understood that even in these three modes, the touch of the implied meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*) alone is the cause of the beauty of poetry. As the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* said: "In every way, there is no mode of poetry that captivates the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdaya*) which does not possess charm through contact with the implied meaning."

Therefore, this supreme secret of poetry should be contemplated by the wise. "This suggested shadow (pratīyamānacchāyā) is the primary ornament of the words of great poets, even when they already possess [other] ornaments; it is like the modesty of women. Furthermore, that same type of poetry is seen as another variety where the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), wherein the beauty of the expressed meaning becomes preeminent through its connection with the suggested.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that this term *dhvani* is intended merely to indicate its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) with respect to its possible occurrence, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to demonstrate other elements contained within that same sentence—such as words, phonemes, and their number—as well, since there is no distinction between them. Consequently, this [definition] would result in nothing more than the mere learning of the relationship between a name and the thing named, and thus it would not have the fruit of teaching the specific nature of poetry. Nor does the fact that these [other elements] are presented as subordinate prevent their being inferable.

Thus, in this way, it is not the case that meaning and word have their own primary meanings subordinated [in poetry], because that would be corrupted by the defects of inconsistency and impossibility. Nor can there be a relationship of the manifestor (vyañjaka) and the manifested (vyaṅgya) between the expressed (vācya) and the implied (pratīyamāna), because the defining characteristics of such a relationship are absent. Furthermore, there is no purpose in providing a definition for a specific type of poetry [if it lacks such a relationship]. Nor is the designation "dhvani" tenable in the absence of a relationship between the manifestor and the manifested. Consequently, its entire definition appears to be entirely inconsistent.
If beauty is indeed desired even in poetry where the implied is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya), then any regard for "dhvani" as possessing excellence is utterly futile. (96)
For there is no possibility of *dhvani*, which constitutes the very soul of poetry, existing therein;
therefore, it would be as if lifeless, so what talk can there be of its excellence? (97)

Therefore, those who asserted the non-existence of sound—which is not of the nature of that [ether]—have been refuted in vain, as they failed to perceive the inherent nature of their own statement. 98.
If that [status of being poetry] is not accepted even there, it would be in relation to the manifestation of rasa and so forth;
otherwise, this [work] would not be poetry at all, since it consists essentially of rasa. (99)

And thus, when there is a mere touch of the implied meaning upon the expressed, that would be what is called "ornamentation"; therefore, that very [ornament] would be considered inference (anumā). 100.

These are the summary verses. Furthermore, regarding the two types of *dhvani* mentioned—namely, that whose expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣita-vācya*) and that whose expressed meaning is intended but subordinate to another (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācya*)—one must state its meaning according to its essential purport: what indeed is this "unintendedness"? Is it non-acceptability, or is it being subordinate to something else? And as for non-acceptability, is it total or partial? If it were non-acceptability in its entirety, then its capacity to suggest (*vyañjakatva*) would also have to be rejected, because that [suggestive power] is dependent upon it.

Consequently, its very formulation would be defective, just as that of another [fault] such as redundancy (*punarukta*). If it is argued that [the fault applies] only in part, then that "part" must be specified; yet, when examined, it ultimately resolves into nothing other than the lack of primacy [of the literal meaning]. Therefore, since "not being intended to be expressed," "being subordinate to something else," and "having one's own nature made secondary" are synonymous, this manner of expression merely states the essential nature of *dhvani* itself, and not a classification of its types.

For when a particular sub-distinction (antara-viśeṣa) is touched upon while following the general definition of something, that is called its "mode" (prakāra); for example, the quality of being a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) is a mode of "cowness. However, it is not possible for that very same thing to be its own mode, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Since there is no touch with any such sub-distinction here, how can the statement that sound is a "mode" of this [meaning] be considered logical? Furthermore, we do not understand what this so-called "intendedness of a meaning other than the literal" (*vivakṣitānyapara-vācyatva*) actually is.

If "intendedness" (*vivakṣitatva*) is said to constitute primacy (*prādhānya*), then how can it be consistent for that same thing to be subordinate to something else (*anyaparatva*)? For subordination to another is defined as being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*). And how could that which is an auxiliary simultaneously experience primacy by virtue of being intended? Thus, the claim that the expressed meaning is both intended and subordinate to another is contradictory, because intendedness and subordination to another are mutually exclusive.

For the connection between primacy and its opposite is logically consistent only with respect to an object intended as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) when they share a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*), and not with respect to other objects. That very [qualifier] possesses primacy because it is intended as the basis for imparting excellence to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). And by virtue of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is capable of experiencing non-primacy in a real sense. For example: "O right hand! Release the sword upon the Śūdra ascetic for the sake of reviving the dead Brahmin boy!"

"O hand of Rāma, you are skilled in the banishment of Sītā when she was exhausted by her heavy pregnancy; where is your compassion? Thus it is said in the *Uttararāmacarita*. Furthermore, if this [poem] is accepted as a variety of *dhvani* characterized by a "suggested sense other than the literal" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), then the "other-directedness" of the literal sense (*vācya*) would be redundant, since that very status is established by its being a variety of *dhvani*. For "other-directedness" is the state of having the literal meaning made subordinate; and that has already been stated to be the general definition of *dhvani*.

Just as that [quality] is adopted here, so too should it be adopted in the previous case, or else it should not be adopted in either case, since there is no difference in both being modes of that [quality]. Furthermore, the example given for the type of suggestion where the expressed meaning is transferred to another object (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) is consistent only with the figurative function based on qualities (*guṇavṛtti*), because that is established as a mode of figurative function based on qualities. For instance, metaphor (*upacāra*) is the superimposition of one thing onto another for the sake of perceiving a similarity between them, provided that the other thing possesses a well-known state of neither deficiency nor excess [in its qualities].

This [superimposition] should be understood as having both meanings as its object, consisting as it does in the nature of the relationship between the superimposed and the superimposer. Consequently, when a single meaning denoted by a single word assumes the status of an object for this [metaphor] in a dual form—through the conceptualization of general and particular aspects—then it is precisely the particular aspect, in which excellence or deficiency has been determined according to the context of the meaning and so forth, that becomes the cause for the perception of similarity through superimposition; as in the examples: "That is nectar, [but] this is nectar," or "He is the moon, [but] this is the moon."

But the universal aspect [is not indicated] by the particular, because the universal does not deviate from the particular. Even that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another object (arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya) is included within inference itself. For words such as "Rāma" convey the bearer of the name (*saṃjñin*) as qualified by attributes—such as excellence or deficiency—which are determined through context and other factors, and not merely the bearer of the name alone.

That other object which is inferred in the form of a property (*dharma*) is to be understood as having been transferred there or transformed into the state of being its substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, the inferable object (*anumeya-artha*) is twofold: in the form of a property and in the form of a substratum. Of these, the former is the domain of this [suggestion], because it is perceived as being grounded precisely in the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*). The latter, however, belongs to another [type of inference], such as "there is fire here because of smoke. Therefore, when a specific property is to be understood, the context and so forth alone should be recognized as the cause, and not words such as "Rāma."

The *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (type where the expressed meaning is completely set aside), however, is merely a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of word-meanings, as in the example "the Vāhīka is an ox. Its inclusion within inference (*anumāna*) has indeed already been established. But the type of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) based on the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) is simply not possible; for it is asserted—and will be further explained—that no other power of the word is admitted apart from its denotative power (*abhidhā*).
Therefore, it is not logical for the *dhvani* in which the expressed meaning is unintended (*avivakṣitavācya*) to have [these two] as its varieties.
For it is not tenable that a thing can be a variety of itself. (101)
Devotion (bhakti) is considered to be of two kinds, consisting of the meaning of individual words and the meaning of the sentence;
and the cognition thereof has been demonstrated to be included within inference. 102.
What, then, is the difference between that [type of] suggestion where the expressed meaning is set aside (tiraskṛtavācya) and [the category of] poetic figure (bhakti)?
Furthermore, how can the second type [of suggestion] be consistent [with it]? (103)

Because the intention [of the speaker] and the state of being directed toward that [intention] are mutually contradictory, that other variety of Dhvani described as being rooted in the power of words [is untenable]. (104)

Thus, this cognition regarding another desired object there is necessarily due to something else, because it has been demonstrated more than once that no other capacity exists within the word itself. (105)
Thus end the summary verses.
Thus concludes the first chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Definition of Dhvani," in the *Vyaktiviveka*, a treatise on poetic figures composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Mahimabhaṭṭa.
